Without specifying location and time, asserting 'much more than 50 percent' is not justified by general evidence and is likely false in many contexts.

claim: The last three days of early voting "happen to be the most populated days of voting that we have in early voting."
rationale: The statement is presented as a general rule but is not universally true. While many jurisdictions do experience heavier turnout in the final days (final weekend and last day) of in-person early voting, turnout patterns vary widely by state, election, and the availability of mail ballots, so the blanket claim is misleading without specifying location and election.

claim: Wisconsin’s economy has "tanked" under Gov. Scott Walker and "so far in 2015 over 6,685 people have been laid off, already more than in all of 2014."
rationale: The assertion that Wisconsin's economy "has tanked" under Gov. Walker is contradicted by state and federal labor statistics through 2015 showing net job gains and a falling unemployment rate. The specific claim that "so far in 2015 over 6,685 people have been laid off, already more than in all of 2014" lacks a documented source and is inconsistent with statewide employment trends and official layoff/WARN data summaries for that period.

claim: Says a photo shows a white man smiling while holding a black man with a bloody face.
rationale: There is insufficient information to verify this description without the actual image or a credible source; claims about people’s race, facial expression, and injury in an unprovided photo are easily miscaptioned or doctored. Because the item is unspecified and unverifiable, I treat the assertion as not proven. If the image and provenance are provided it could be independently authenticated or refuted.

claim: Alaska Sens. Lisa Murkowski and Mark Begich "vote as much as 80 percent of the time together."
rationale: Analyses of Senate roll-call voting during Mark Begich's 2009–2015 term show a high rate of agreement with Lisa Murkowski, often around 75–85% depending on the year and which votes are counted. Public fact-checks and voting-alignment summaries cited figures near 80%, so the claim that they vote as much as 80% of the time together is accurate in that context.

claim: U.S. Rep. Connie Mack "voted to raise his own pay several times."
rationale: There is no clear record showing a U.S. Representative named Connie Mack repeatedly voting to raise his own pay. Congressional pay changes are tied to specific bills and are relatively infrequent; the claim fails to identify which Connie Mack (III or IV) or which votes, and public roll-call records do not support the assertion that a Rep. Connie Mack voted several times to increase congressional salaries.

claim: "Tim Kaine doubled down in his support of devastating defense cuts, saying the ‘the deal was the right thing to do.’"
rationale: There is no verifiable record that Senator Tim Kaine 'doubled down' in support of what are objectively described as 'devastating defense cuts' while saying the exact quote 'the deal was the right thing to do.' Reporting and Kaine's public remarks around budget and debt negotiations through mid‑2024 do not support that specific phrasing or the characterization without additional context. The claim mixes a purported quote with a loaded description without sourcing.

claim: "On my last trip to New Hampshire, I think I met the guy who founded the first and only bank since Dodd-Frank passed, since the financial crisis. One bank in the country."
rationale: The claim that only one bank has been founded in the U.S. since Dodd-Frank (after the financial crisis) is incorrect. While de novo bank approvals dropped immediately after the crisis, regulators have approved numerous new bank charters in the years since 2010, including community banks and newer online/fintech banks. Therefore it is not true that there has been only one bank founded in the country since Dodd-Frank.

claim: Polling shows that nearly 74 percent of National Rifle Association members "support requiring background checks for all gun sales."
rationale: While many national polls find that large majorities of Americans — and even many gun owners — support universal background checks, I could not verify a specific, reliable poll showing 'nearly 74 percent' of National Rifle Association members endorsing that exact formulation. Percentages for NRA members vary across surveys and depend heavily on question wording and sampling, so the precise 74% claim is unsubstantiated without a cited poll.

claim: "In (Sen. Marco) Rubio's state of Florida alone, Social Security lifts more than -- count it -- a million people out of poverty."
rationale: Social Security (retirement and disability benefits) is estimated by the Social Security Administration to lift on the order of tens of millions of people out of poverty nationally; prorating that national impact to Florida’s large share of elderly beneficiaries makes it very likely that more than one million Floridians are kept above the poverty line by Social Security. State-level breakdowns and demographic patterns (Florida’s high share of retirees) support the claim’s magnitude.

claim: Says Donald Trump indicted Amy Coney Barrett.
rationale: There is no evidence that Amy Coney Barrett has been criminally indicted, and a U.S. president (or former president) does not have the legal authority to issue indictments. Indictments are brought by prosecutors or grand juries, and public records and reporting do not show any indictment of Justice Barrett by Donald Trump or anyone else.

claim: "The race will tighten, just because that's what happens at the end of campaigns. They always have."
rationale: This is an overbroad generalization. While many campaigns do see late movement as undecided voters break and events shift sentiment, it is not inevitable—some races remain steady or even see the leader expand their margin through the end. Saying "they always have" is incorrect.

claim: Says unsuccessful Texas abortion legislation "was supported by a majority of" Texans.
rationale: The claim is too general and not supported by available public-opinion evidence: polls around high-profile unsuccessful Texas abortion measures (for example heartbeat-style bans) generally showed divided opinion or majority opposition to strict new limits rather than majority support. Because the statement lacks a named bill and timeframe, there is no convincing evidence that a majority of Texans backed an unspecified unsuccessful abortion bill.

claim: Says "every school will be negatively impacted" if Education Stability Fund is not tapped.
rationale: The blanket assertion that "every school will be negatively impacted" if an Education Stability Fund is not tapped is implausible. Whether schools are affected depends on the size of the shortfall, jurisdictional funding formulas, availability of local reserves or federal grants, and timing, so some schools could avoid immediate negative impacts while others might be hurt.

claim: "Klein did not hold a single town hall meeting (on health care) where the general public was invited to ask questions or present their views."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that Klein never held any town hall meetings on health care; contemporary reporting and historical accounts indicate that during healthcare reforms his government participated in public consultations and held forums where members of the public could ask questions and express views. While formats and organizers varied (some meetings were framed as stakeholder consultations or community forums), it is not accurate to say there were zero such public meetings.

claim: "We have 25 million Americans out of work."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and generally misleading without a date or definition of "out of work." Official Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data do not show a contemporaneous, sustained figure of exactly 25 million officially unemployed Americans; at the COVID-19 peak in spring 2020 the unemployed count was roughly 23 million and initial jobless claims briefly exceeded 25 million cumulatively, but those are different measures.

claim: "We raised the minimum wage to $15 first in city government. Now, working together with people in Albany, it's the law of the state."
rationale: The statement claims the speaker’s city was the first to raise the minimum wage to $15 and that the state later followed; that is misleading. Multiple U.S. cities (for example Seattle and SeaTac) adopted $15 ordinances before many state-level laws, and whether a state later set $15 depends on the specific state and timing. Without naming the city and state the ‘‘first’’ claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: Before COVID-19, "Iowa had one of the lowest unemployment rates in the country, and many employers were scrambling to find qualified employees to fill their job openings."
rationale: In the months immediately before the COVID-19 shutdowns (late 2019–early 2020) Iowa's unemployment rate was among the lowest of U.S. states, reflecting a very tight labor market. Contemporary employer surveys and news reports from Iowa described difficulty recruiting qualified workers in sectors such as manufacturing, healthcare, and construction, consistent with 'employers scrambling' language.

claim: "Obama certificate a fake."
rationale: The claim that Barack Obama's birth certificate is fake has been thoroughly investigated and debunked: the State of Hawaii released a certified long-form birth certificate in 2011 and Hawaii officials have affirmed its authenticity. Multiple independent fact-checkers, journalists, and state authorities found no credible evidence of forgery.

claim: Video shows helicopters in Ukraine "being picked off in ambush - Short range air-to-air missile"
rationale: There is insufficient verifiable evidence to support the specific claim that the clip shows helicopters in Ukraine being shot by a short‑range air‑to‑air missile in an ambush. Open‑source verification requires provenance, geolocation, timestamps, and expert munition analysis; many similar videos have been misattributed and instead show ground‑launched MANPADS or anti‑aircraft fire. Absent corroborating metadata or independent verification, the specific weapon type and circumstances cannot be reliably established.

claim: "Wayfair CEO steps down."
rationale: The statement is presented without date or named individual and, based on available information up to my last reliable update, there were no widely reported departures of Wayfair's CEO. Wayfair's CEO (Niraj Shah as of mid‑2024) remaining in place was the last confirmed status, so the bare claim lacks supporting evidence.

claim: "We have the highest per-pupil cost in the country."
rationale: The claim is vague because it does not identify who "we" refers to or which year is meant. National data from sources that track per‑pupil spending show the top spenders vary by year (commonly D.C., New York, Alaska, or select states), so a blanket statement that "we have the highest per‑pupil cost in the country" cannot be verified and is unlikely to be true without specifying the jurisdiction and time period.

claim: President Barack Obama’s health care reform "slashed $500 billion from Medicare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included roughly $500 billion in reductions to projected Medicare spending over about a decade, according to CBO and the Medicare actuary, but those were mainly cuts to provider and plan payments, fraud reduction, and payment reforms—not direct cuts to beneficiaries' Medicare benefits. Saying it "slashed $500 billion from Medicare" implies benefits were cut by that amount, which is misleading.

claim: The media has "a lower approval rate than Congress."
rationale: The claim is presented as a general fact but lacks timeframe, poll source, and definition of "the media." Public-opinion measures for Congress and for the news media vary by poll and over time; sometimes surveys show media rated lower, sometimes Congress is rated lower. Without a specified survey and period, the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: The streetcar project planned by Mayor Tom Barrett would be a "1900s style trolley."
rationale: The streetcar project advanced under Mayor Tom Barrett specified modern, low-floor, ADA-compliant streetcars built to contemporary light-rail standards rather than restored or replica early-1900s vintage trolleys. Vehicles procured for the Milwaukee streetcar program were modern designs (United Streetcar based on current LRV technology), so calling the project a '1900s style trolley' is inaccurate.

claim: "There's only four senators senior to me ... there's still 44 older than me."
rationale: The claim gives two numeric assertions about Senate seniority and age but omits who is speaking and when, so it cannot be independently verified as stated. Whether those exact counts are true depends entirely on a specific senator and date; without that context the statement is effectively uncheckable and should be treated as false for verification purposes.

claim: "If every house in Florida had a solar-heated water tank, that would eliminate consumption by 17 percent."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and unlikely to be correct as written. While water heating is often cited as roughly 15–20% of a typical household's energy use, statewide energy consumption includes commercial, industrial, transportation and other uses so converting every home to solar water heaters would not eliminate 17% of Florida's total energy consumption; additionally solar water heaters usually reduce but do not entirely eliminate auxiliary heating needs.

claim: Says Bruce Poliquin "voted to strip 117,000 Mainers of their insurance."
rationale: While Bruce Poliquin supported Republican bills that would have rolled back significant parts of the Affordable Care Act (for example the House AHCA in 2017), there is no authoritative evidence that he cast a vote that directly and immediately "stripped 117,000 Mainers of their insurance." State-level loss estimates vary by model and depend on bills becoming law; a member's vote for a bill that might increase the uninsured is not the same as a verified, direct stripping of coverage for an exact number of people.

claim: "The CDC director just said that 75% of ‘Covid deaths’ occurred in people with at least four comorbidities."
rationale: There is no reliable record of the CDC director making a recent statement that 75% of COVID deaths occurred in people with at least four comorbidities. CDC reports do show that many decedents had one or more underlying conditions, but the agency’s published distributions do not support a blanket claim that three-quarters had ≥4 comorbidities and this appears to be a misquote or misinterpretation of CDC data.

claim: "Women in Oregon are paid 79 cents for every dollar paid to men. If the wage gap was eliminated, a working woman in Oregon would have enough money for 2,877 gallons of gas, 72 more weeks of food for her family or nearly 12 more months of rent."
rationale: The headline number (women in Oregon paid 79 cents per dollar) can be true for specific years or particular measurement methods, but pay-gap figures vary by data source and year and are sensitive to whether they compare median annual earnings, hourly wages, full‑time workers, or all workers. The specific claims about 2,877 gallons of gas, 72 weeks of food, or nearly 12 months of rent require unstated assumptions about the baseline earnings, time period (presumably annual), and assumed prices for gas, food and rent; without those assumptions the dollar-to-goods conversions cannot be independently verified. Because the statement mixes a plausible but time- and method-dependent statistic with precise conversions that lack documented assumptions, I rate the overall composite claim as not reliably supported as presented.

claim: "The Democrat controlled House never even asked John Bolton to testify."
rationale: This is incorrect: during the Trump impeachment process the Democratic-majority House and its committees sought John Bolton’s testimony and there were public calls and legal steps to obtain it (including threats of subpoena and requests by House investigators). Bolton initially resisted cooperating voluntarily and legal wrangling occurred, but Democrats did ask him to testify. The claim misstates the record.

claim: "Overdoses in Virginia (are) up 35%."
rationale: The statement is too vague to be verified as written — it gives no timeframe, metric (fatal vs nonfatal overdoses), or data source. Official Virginia and federal overdose reports show variable year-to-year changes and regionally different increases; while some periods during the COVID era saw substantial rises in some categories, there is no unqualified, universally applicable finding that 'overdoses in Virginia are up 35%.'

claim: "I have returned money every year since taking office."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because the speaker is not identified and the phrase "returned money" is ambiguous (could mean returned salary, refunded campaign donations, returned unspent appropriations, etc.). Without a named officeholder, dates, amounts, and public records or documentation, there is no way to confirm the universal assertion "every year since taking office." Therefore I rate the claim as false due to lack of verifiable evidence.

claim: In Milwaukee, "murder is up an astonishing 57 percent."
rationale: The statement gives no timeframe or baseline, so it is not verifiable as a general fact. Milwaukee homicide rates have fluctuated year-to-year and some short windows (monthly or year-to-date comparisons) have shown very large percentage increases, but there is no persistent, unqualified 57% increase across standard reporting periods.

claim: "Last week, the Colorado Supreme Court declared that Boulder’s AR-15 ban was unconstitutional. Today, there was a mass shooting in Boulder."
rationale: I cannot confirm either part of this claim because my training data ends in June 2024 and I have no access to real-time news; I have no reliable record in my knowledge that the Colorado Supreme Court recently struck down Boulder's AR-15 ban. Because I cannot verify a reported court decision 'last week' or a 'today' mass shooting in Boulder, the composite claim should not be accepted without current independent news or court records.

claim: "The Simpsons" predicted Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
rationale: There is no episode of The Simpsons that explicitly and accurately forecasted Russia’s 2022 large-scale invasion of Ukraine; viral clips claiming a prediction are either taken out of context, depict fictional or generic geopolitical jokes, or show coincidental imagery. The show is satirical and has occasionally included scenes involving Russia or fictional invasions, but these are not specific, verifiable predictions of the real 2022 event.

claim: Says Nelson Mandela "was a communist."
rationale: Calling Mandela straightforwardly "a communist" is misleading. He cooperated closely with the South African Communist Party, accepted communist support, and held socialist-leaning views, but he repeatedly denied formal SACP membership and definitive proof of card-carrying membership is contested.

claim: Says with "Gov. Chris Christie and bipartisan reformers" New Jersey had "the most job growth in 11 years."
rationale: The statement is vague and not supported as a blanket fact: while New Jersey did add jobs during Gov. Chris Christie’s tenure, independent BLS and New Jersey Department of Labor series do not unambiguously show that NJ had “the most job growth in 11 years” without specifying the exact 11‑year window, whether private vs. total jobs, and the month/year being compared. Such claims have often been selective about the time frame or metric to produce the largest-sounding gain and therefore are misleading as stated.

claim: "If you give guns to gangs, you can get out of jail free, if (California’s Proposition 57) passes. If you do a drive-by shooting, you can get out of jail free, if Proposition 57 passes. If you discharge guns on a school yard, you can get out of jail free."
rationale: California Proposition 57 does not grant an automatic "get out of jail free" release for violent crimes; it provides parole consideration and earned credit for rehabilitation only for inmates convicted of nonviolent felonies. Crimes like drive-by shootings or discharging a firearm on a schoolyard are typically charged as violent felonies or serious offenses and are excluded from Prop 57's parole-eligibility provisions. The measure also does not automatically erase convictions or force immediate release without review.

claim: "#GradInsurance debacle is a DIRECT result of #ObamaCare. #MIZZOU has to break the law to do the right thing."
rationale: The claim asserts that a graduate student insurance problem at Mizzou was a direct result of the Affordable Care Act and that the university must "break the law" to resolve it. There is no clear evidence that ACA directly caused such a specific administrative debacle; problems with campus insurance are typically due to institutional decisions, plan administration, or state rules, and universities generally have lawful compliance options and exemptions. Saying the school "has to break the law" is a normative/legal claim with no supporting factual basis.

claim: "In ‘Resident Evil’ the Umbrella Corporation releases a virus that infects the people of Raccoon City. A biological research lab with the exact same logo as the Umbrella Corporation can be found in the city where the coronavirus outbreak originated."
rationale: While Resident Evil’s Umbrella Corporation is fictional and does release a virus in Raccoon City, there is no credible evidence that a real-world biological research lab in the city where the COVID-19 outbreak began uses the Umbrella Corporation logo. Images and claims circulating online showing such a logo have been debunked or shown to be misidentifications or edits.

claim: Says 1 in 5 Texans did not have health insurance coverage before the pandemic, and now "nearly 1 in 3 Texans under the age of 65 don’t have access to health care insurance."
rationale: The first part is roughly correct: pre-pandemic (around 2018–2019) Texas had an uninsured rate near 17–20%, about 1 in 5 people. The second part — that "nearly 1 in 3 Texans under the age of 65" currently lack access to health insurance (~33%) — is not supported by available state-level survey data, which show uninsured rates well below one-third for Texans under 65 in recent years.

claim: Health care reform will not affect veterans' benefits.
rationale: Saying health care reform will not affect veterans' benefits is incorrect as a blanket statement. Veterans' benefits are administered separately, but reforms frequently change insurance eligibility, funding flows, provider networks, or care coordination (for example, the Affordable Care Act's Medicaid expansion and new private coverage options altered how some veterans obtained or supplemented care). Whether a specific reform changes legal entitlements versus practical access depends on the law's details.

claim: "1928 was last time Republicans had the White House, the House and the Senate."
rationale: This is incorrect: Republicans controlled the White House, the House, and the Senate after the 2002 midterm elections (with President George W. Bush and GOP majorities in both chambers in the 108th Congress, 2003–2007). Therefore 1928 was not the last time Republicans held all three simultaneously.

claim: Mehmet Oz "was a spokesman for a group who wanted to defund the police."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Mehmet Oz served as a spokesman for any organization that called to "defund the police." Oz has been primarily known as a television physician, founder of health nonprofits, and a Republican Senate candidate who publicly criticized the 'defund the police' movement. The claim appears to conflate or misattribute positions to him without supporting documentation.

claim: Says abortion is "the leading cause of death for black Americans and kills as many as 1,000 black children every day."
rationale: Public health data do not support that abortion is the leading cause of death for Black Americans, and the claim of 1,000 Black children killed every day greatly overstates the numbers. National mortality statistics list heart disease and cancer as the top causes of death for Black Americans, and major abortion surveillance estimates (CDC and Guttmacher) show annual abortions of Black women are substantially lower than 365,000 (1,000 per day). The claim also conflates fetuses with counted deaths in standard mortality data, a methodological inconsistency.

claim: Says a "Pro-Stimulus economist admits it is not working … "
rationale: The claim as presented lacks any specific attribution, quote, or context (which economist, which stimulus, when), so it cannot be verified. Without a named source or evidence, the assertion that a “pro‑stimulus economist admits it is not working” is unsubstantiated; while some economists who generally support stimulus may criticize particular programs, that is not equivalent to a general admission that stimulus is failing.

claim: "Right to Work states have: faster private sector employment growth"
rationale: The empirical evidence is mixed and does not consistently support the general statement that right-to-work (RTW) laws cause faster private-sector employment growth. Some studies find positive associations, but those results are often sensitive to methodology and are confounded by other factors (population growth, industry mix, tax and regulatory differences, and migration).

claim: "We have one of the most expensive General Assemblies, per capita, in the entire country."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as phrased because it does not name the state, timeframe, or how 'expensive' is being measured (salaries, staff, benefits, total budget, etc.). Per-capita legislative costs vary widely across states and depend on many definitional choices, so without a specific source or metric the broad claim cannot be substantiated and is therefore judged false.

claim: Congressman Scott DesJarlais "is spending his one year anniversary on vacation -- only working 6 days in all of January."
rationale: The statement is specific but provides no year or source and I cannot confirm it from public records. Congressional calendars, roll-call votes, and official member schedules (which are public) would be needed to prove he worked only six days in a given January; without a date or corroborating reporting this claim is unverified and therefore likely false.

claim: Says Mitt Romney belittled middle-class tax cuts "as nothing more than 'little Band-Aids.' "
rationale: I am not aware of any reliable record in Romney's public statements where he explicitly called middle-class tax cuts "nothing more than 'little Band-Aids.'" Political opponents have sometimes paraphrased or amplified his critiques of short-term fixes, but that exact quoted phrasing appears to be a misattribution or partisan framing rather than a direct Romney quote.

claim: "This past (legislative) session, we passed out of the Legislature a resolution requiring Congress to pass a balanced-budget amendment to the (U.S.) Constitution."
rationale: No state legislature can legally compel Congress to pass a constitutional amendment. State legislatures can adopt nonbinding resolutions urging Congress to act or can apply for an Article V convention to propose amendments, but such measures do not 'require' Congress to pass an amendment.

claim: "The 2008 election was the first election in which voters of color comprised over 25 percent of the electorate, and that number is going up."
rationale: Census and election analyses show 2008 was the first presidential election in which non-Hispanic white voters fell below about 75% of the electorate, meaning voters of color exceeded 25%. Subsequent elections have generally shown an increasing share of Black, Hispanic, Asian, and other nonwhite voters, continuing the upward trend in electorate diversity.

claim: "Wages are on the rise — in fact we were the top small-business wage growth state in the nation."
rationale: The statement is too specific (being “the top small-business wage growth state”) but gives no state, timeframe, or data source, and available wage-growth rankings differ by dataset and period. Different measures (BLS, ADP, Paychex, Census) and differing definitions of “small business” produce different state rankings, so the unqualified claim cannot be verified and is likely misleading without supporting data.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty is endorsed by the Austin American-Statesman.
rationale: There is no evidence in known endorsement records or reporting that the Austin American-Statesman has endorsed anyone named Gerald Daugherty. Major newspapers' public endorsement lists and past coverage of local races do not include that name, so the claim is unsupported.

claim: Says David Dewhurst skipped nine candidate forums after announcing his U.S. Senate candidacy.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific assertion that David Dewhurst skipped nine candidate forums after announcing his U.S. Senate candidacy; contemporaneous coverage noted he missed some debates and events during the 2012 Texas Senate race, but the exact count 'nine' is unconfirmed and appears to vary by source and by how 'forums' are defined. Because the precise number is not reliably supported, the claim as stated is not verified.

claim: "Florida spends more than $300 million a year just on children repeating pre-K through 3rd grade."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence that Florida spends more than $300 million annually solely on children repeating pre-K through 3rd grade. Cost claims of this type depend heavily on definitions (direct instructional cost vs. total system cost), per-pupil spending assumptions, and the number of retained students, and available state reporting and analyses do not substantiate the specific $300M figure. Without a cited source the claim is unverified and likely overstated.

claim: "Marco Rubio made it clear: Not only does he think Donald Trump is a con man, he went on to say he doesn't trust Donald Trump with the nuclear codes."
rationale: Marco Rubio has criticized Donald Trump on temperament and honesty at times, but there is no well-documented public record of Rubio using the specific lines that Trump is a “con man” and explicitly saying he “doesn't trust Donald Trump with the nuclear codes.” Other Republicans have used the nuclear‑codes line, but attributing that exact double statement to Rubio appears inaccurate or unverified.

claim: Richmond is "the most vegan-friendly city."
rationale: The claim is unqualified and subjective; there is no widely accepted evidence that any place named Richmond is the single "most vegan-friendly city." Rankings of vegan-friendliness depend on metrics (number of vegan restaurants, product availability, policy, community), and commonly cited lists favor cities like Portland, Los Angeles, Berlin, and New York over Richmond. Without clear definition or authoritative ranking placing a specific Richmond at the top, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "There's been no conclusive or specific report to say" Russia was trying to muddy the election.
rationale: U.S. intelligence agencies and criminal indictments have concluded Russia conducted active measures to influence and sow discord around U.S. elections. Investigations and assessments (notably related to 2016 and assessments around 2020) documented efforts by Russian actors to spread disinformation, amplify divisive content, and interfere with electoral processes, which contradicts the claim that there are no conclusive or specific reports.

claim: Says Measure 3-386 will cost a fortune for elections while Measure 3-388 will cost less.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as presented because measure numbers alone are ambiguous and no jurisdiction or year is given. Whether one ballot measure 'will cost a fortune' versus another 'will cost less' requires official fiscal impact estimates and implementation details, which are not provided. Without a specific, cited fiscal analysis, the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "I cut more as a percentage out of government than any state in the country this past decade. And where is Michigan in terms of its economic growth? Cutting did not result in economic growth."
rationale: The assertion that Michigan cut a larger share of government spending than any state over the past decade is unsubstantiated and depends on precise timeframe and measurement; other states implemented deeper proportional cuts in various years. Moreover, Michigan experienced notable post-recession economic recovery (auto-sector rebound and job/GDP gains) during the 2010s, so the blanket claim that cutting did not result in economic growth is not supported without clearer metrics.

claim: "Fifty percent of the Ottawa police force have all turned in their resignation."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official confirmations that 50% of the Ottawa Police Service resigned; such a mass resignation would have been extensively covered by major news outlets and city officials. Public statements and reporting do not support this claim.

claim: Anthony Fauci was on the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years and "currently serves on Gates Foundation."
rationale: Anthony Fauci has not served on the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years and is not a current board member of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. Official leadership rosters and multiple reputable fact-checks show Fauci's career is as a federal public-health official and advisor, not as a long-term board member of those foundations; he has collaborated with or been funded by various foundations but that is not equivalent to board service.

claim: "California is 49th out of 50 in the United States in per capita housing units. Only Utah can lay claim to being lowest in per capita production."
rationale: The statement is unsupported and ambiguous: rankings depend on the exact metric and year. Official Census/HUD data do not consistently place California 49th in housing units per capita, and other states (e.g., New York, Massachusetts) can rank as low or lower depending on the measure. The phrase 'per capita production' is undefined, so the claim that only Utah is lower cannot be verified without a specific dataset and time period.

claim: "McCain opposes repeal of the death tax."
rationale: The claim is too categorical without a timeframe or which 'McCain' is meant. John McCain's public positions on the estate tax (often called the 'death tax') shifted over time—he sometimes supported reductions or repeal proposals and at other times opposed full repeal for fiscal or policy reasons—so a blanket statement that 'McCain opposes repeal' is inaccurate without context. Because the record is mixed, the claim as presented is misleading.

claim: The Baucus health care bill "would drastically restrict the use of flexible spending accounts (FSAs) in order to help pay for health care reform."
rationale: Sen. Max Baucus's health-care proposal included a provision to cap tax-free flexible spending account (FSA) contributions (commonly cited as $2,500), which would limit the pre-tax amount individuals could set aside for medical expenses and was presented as an offset to help pay for reform. Describing this as a restriction is accurate, though the adjective "drastically" is subjective and impacts perceived severity.

claim: "Hidden in the CARES Act was an obscure $135 billion tax break for 43,000 millionaires."
rationale: The $135 billion figure stems from an upper‑bound estimate tied to CARES Act net operating loss (NOL) carryback rules, not a clear, direct 'tax break' exclusively for 43,000 millionaires. The provision applied to corporations and pass‑through businesses and could generate refunds, but the $135B was a maximum scenario and the claim that it secretly benefited 43,000 millionaires is misleading—beneficiaries were businesses and the estimate is uncertain. The change was also an explicit, widely reported part of the law, not a hidden item.

claim: "They’ve seen employer-supported coverage increase in Massachusetts after this law (Romneycare) was implemented."
rationale: Empirical analyses of Massachusetts' 2006 health reform show large increases in overall coverage driven by Medicaid and subsidized individual plans, not by growth in employer-sponsored insurance. Most national and state assessments (Census/ACS and research from think tanks) found employer-sponsored coverage stayed flat or declined modestly after the law, while public and individual coverage rose.

claim: "The cost-of-living increase in Social Security is tied to wage inflation."
rationale: The annual Social Security cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in the U.S. is tied to changes in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which measures price inflation, not wage inflation. Wage growth (average wage index) is used for wage-indexing benefits and some tax thresholds but does not determine the COLA.

claim: "Cities in notoriously ‘tough on crime’ states like Texas and Florida saw a more significant increase in violent crime than cities in NYS."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and not supported by available reporting: violent crime trends vary substantially by city and by year, and there is no consistent nationwide pattern showing that cities in Texas and Florida experienced larger increases than cities in New York State as a whole. Some cities in Texas and Florida did see large rises, but other cities in those states did not, and several New York State cities also saw notable increases in particular years. Without a specified timeframe, list of cities, and whether rates or raw counts are compared, the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: The unemployment rate may be as high as "42 percent."
rationale: The claim as stated is unsupported because it gives no country, time period, or definition of unemployment; most national overall unemployment rates do not reach 42%. While some countries or specific groups (for example youth unemployment in a crisis) have approached or exceeded 40%, presenting a blanket figure of "may be as high as 42 percent" is misleading without context. Therefore the unqualified claim is false.

claim: "Al-Qaida operatives, have said, 'Hey, we want you to use this loophole (for purchasing guns despite being on a watch list) to attack and kill Americans.'"
rationale: There is no credible public evidence that al-Qaida operatives have been documented saying that exact line encouraging use of a purchase loophole to buy guns while on a watch list. While extremist groups have urged followers to carry out attacks and sometimes discuss exploiting vulnerabilities, the specific quoted claim appears unverified and not attributable to a reliable primary source.

claim: "Over 97 percent of the scientific community … believe that humans are contributing to climate change."
rationale: The commonly cited ~97% figure is supported by multiple analyses showing about 97% of publishing climate scientists or climate-science papers endorse that humans are the primary cause of recent global warming. However, the claim as worded—'97 percent of the scientific community'—overstates the scope: that high percentage refers specifically to climate scientists or peer-reviewed climate literature, not the entire scientific community across all disciplines. Because the phrase is imprecise, the claim is misleading.

claim: Democratic U.S. House candidate Julie Lassa pushed for a "Canadian-style government takeover of health care."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Julie Lassa explicitly advocated adopting a Canadian-style single-payer 'government takeover' of health care. Public records and campaign materials show she supported health-care reform and measures to expand access (such as backing the Affordable Care Act and related reforms), but opponents' ads have described such positions hyperbolically as a 'government takeover.'

claim: Says Ben Carson said "illegal immigrants caught voting should be stripped of their citizenship."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Ben Carson saying the quoted line. In public statements and debates he called for prosecuting or deporting noncitizens who vote, but did not advocate stripping citizenship — a step that generally wouldn't apply to noncitizens and would involve denaturalization for citizens. The claim appears to mischaracterize or exaggerate his actual statements.

claim: "Last year, (Bill McCollum) spent more than $2.2 million dollars to produce and air campaign-style TV ads where you were featured in almost every frame."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim as stated: there is no corroborating public evidence that Bill McCollum spent more than $2.2 million 'last year' to produce and air campaign-style TV ads that featured the addressed person in almost every frame. The statement is imprecise about the year and who 'you' refers to, and no clear campaign finance or media-buy reporting supports that exact figure and description. Without clear, dated records or contemporaneous reporting, the claim is not substantiated.

claim: "California lawmakers are planning to push free abortion pills on all students across the state as part of a ‘super progressive’ new policy."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that California lawmakers are planning a policy that would force or automatically "push" free abortion pills on all students statewide. While California has passed and considered measures to expand access to abortion and to fund provision at clinics and some college health centers, those efforts are about increasing voluntary access and funding — not mandatory distribution to every student.

claim: "The collective net worth of Americans has taken a $5.5 trillion hit ... mainly due to plummeting home values."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no timeframe or source for the $5.5 trillion figure and attributes the loss mainly to falling home values without supporting data. Changes in US household net worth are driven by both housing and financial markets, and in many recent episodes (especially short-term drops) equities and retirement accounts, not home values, were the dominant contributors. Without a specific period and source, the assertion that a $5.5T hit occurred and was mainly due to home values cannot be confirmed.

claim: Tim Tebow used to "kneel in prayer and the NFL complained."
rationale: Tim Tebow was well known for kneeling in prayer on the field after plays (the so‑called "Tebowing"), but there is no record that the NFL as an organization formally complained about or sanctioned him specifically for praying. The league had celebration/taunting rules that prompted occasional discussion about on-field gestures, and some commentators or opponents criticized or questioned the behavior, but that is different from the NFL formally complaining.

claim: "There was never a single shred of evidence presented to anyone" that the attacks in Benghazi, Libya, were "spontaneous, and in fact, the CIA themselves understood that early on."
rationale: The claim is false. In the immediate aftermath there were multiple pieces of evidence and public talking points indicating a link to local demonstrations (including references to an anti‑Islam video) and intelligence reporting was circulated; the CIA’s own assessments were not uniformly certain early on and evolved as more intelligence was collected, ultimately attributing the attack to organized militant groups. Investigations (including the State Department Accountability Review Board, congressional inquiries, and later Intelligence Community reports) show a shifting, contested intelligence picture rather than a single, unanimous early CIA conclusion that it was not spontaneous.

claim: "I am the only member of Congress that voted for both inquiries -- the Clinton inquiry and now the Trump inquiry."
rationale: The claim that a single member was the only member to vote in both the Clinton inquiry (late 1998) and a later Trump inquiry is incorrect. Congressional roll-call records and the fact that many members’ tenures span both periods mean multiple members were eligible and records show more than one member cast votes on both sets of proceedings.

claim: In the 100 days since its passage, the economic stimulus has "saved or created nearly 150,000 jobs."
rationale: The statement reflects an administration estimate that was model-based and presented as jobs "saved or created," not a direct, independently verifiable headcount. Early post-passage claims about the stimulus relied on projections and attribution rules that economists and fact-checkers said were subject to significant uncertainty, so the precise figure of "nearly 150,000" is not a solid, unambiguous fact.

claim: "As a city, we currently use about 4 percent less electricity today than we used in 1989."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as phrased because it does not name which city or cite a data source; electricity consumption trends vary widely so some cities may use less today than in 1989 while others use more. Total city consumption is influenced by population, economic activity, efficiency improvements, and electrification, so an absolute 4% decline claim requires specific utility data to confirm.

claim: Says the Ohio Consumers’ Council office employs 74 lawyers and that the funding them is wasteful duplication.
rationale: The Ohio Consumers' Counsel is a small state consumer-advocacy office that historically employs a modest legal staff far smaller than 74 attorneys; the specific figure of 74 lawyers is implausible and unsupported. The claim that funding them is 'wasteful duplication' is an evaluative judgment, not an objective fact, and ignores the office's statutory role representing residential utility consumers before regulatory bodies.

claim: "Our income, our GDP per capita, is almost 50 percent higher than (it is for) the average European."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unsupported as stated: GDP per capita comparisons depend on which country 'our' refers to and whether figures are nominal or PPP. Depending on the country and comparator, gaps are often smaller than 50% (and for many European countries the statement would be false), while the U.S. is higher than some European averages but the exact gap varies by definition and is not universally 'almost 50%'.

claim: "27 U.S. Air Force pilots resign over COVID-19 vaccination mandate."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that exactly 27 U.S. Air Force pilots resigned specifically in protest of the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. Reporting and official DoD/USAF releases showed only small, scattered separations or administrative actions across services and did not substantiate a mass resignation of 27 pilots; many claims conflated different ranks, time periods, or separations for other reasons.

claim: Under the Hate Crimes bill, "any pastor, preacher, priest, rabbi or imam who gives a sermon out of their moral traditions about sexual practices could be found guilty of a federal crime."
rationale: This is misleading: federal hate‑crime statutes generally criminalize violent acts, threats, or property damage motivated by protected characteristics, not the mere delivery of a sermon expressing traditional moral views about sexual practices. Ordinary religious teaching is protected by the First Amendment; only speech that crosses into true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action, or targeted harassment could support criminal prosecution.

claim: Says Joe Biden said, "This country is doomed, not just because of African Americans, but because by 2040 this country is going to be minority white European."
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or major news report of Joe Biden uttering this line; the wording and sentiment do not match his documented public remarks, which typically frame demographic change in inclusive or neutral terms rather than saying the country is 'doomed' or singling out African Americans. The quote appears to be fabricated or a severe misattribution.

claim: Says "Kurt Schrader supports Obama’s sequester … but won’t cut $1.6 million to fund new video games."
rationale: The statement bundles a general accusation with a specific spending figure but lacks verifiable support. Public congressional voting records do not clearly show a direct vote by Rep. Kurt Schrader described as "supporting Obama's sequester," and there is no clear evidence he explicitly refused to cut a $1.6 million item for "new video games"—the alleged $1.6M item and vote context are not documented. Because the claim mixes ambiguous language and an unreferenced dollar figure, it cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: "We became a net exporter of natural gas in 2017, and until recently, our exports have exceeded our imports."
rationale: The United States did become a net exporter of natural gas in 2017, but the statement's second clause is ambiguous and potentially misleading: U.S. exports continued to exceed imports through multiple subsequent years (at least through 2022–2023 per energy data), so saying "until recently" implies a recent reversal that is not clearly supported. Because the claim mixes a correct historical fact with a vague, unsupported time qualifier, I judge the overall claim false as stated.

claim: "We are not producing jobs. We created 80,000 jobs last month. We don't talk about the jobs that we lost. The net of it all is that we lost jobs."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely incorrect as stated because the commonly reported monthly 'jobs created' figure (from the BLS nonfarm payrolls) already represents the net change in payroll employment for that month. Saying “we created 80,000 jobs last month” but that “the net of it all is that we lost jobs” is contradictory unless referring to different surveys, timeframes, or later revisions—none of which are specified.

claim: Says Steve Jobs said, "I realize that all my recognition and wealth that I have is meaningless in the face of imminent death."
rationale: There is no record of Steve Jobs uttering that exact sentence; it appears to be a paraphrase or summary of themes from his 2005 Stanford commencement address and remarks about mortality. Jobs did speak about death making wealth and recognition feel less important, but the quoted wording is not an attested direct quote.

claim: "Every day, a black name resume is 50 percent less likely to get responded to than a white name resume."
rationale: Field audit experiments have repeatedly found that résumés with Black‑sounding names often receive substantially fewer callbacks than those with White‑sounding names (a high‑profile 2004 study found about a 50% lower callback rate in its sample). However, the blanket statement that this happens "every day" as a universal rule is too absolute: effect sizes vary by occupation, location, time period and study design, so it cannot be asserted as an always‑true daily fact.

claim: "In Wisconsin, only half of all the adults with serious psychological distress received mental health treatment or medication."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim as stated and it is likely inaccurate without a year or data source. Estimates of how many adults with serious psychological distress (SPD) receive treatment vary by survey (BRFSS, NSDUH) and year, and Wisconsin's reported treatment rate in some years has been above 50%; the statement as an absolute claim lacks necessary context.

claim: "A rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months. The legislature’s failure to expand Medicaid has brought crisis to many of Missouri’s rural health care providers."
rationale: The claim mixes an unsupported precise closure rate with a misleading cause. While some rural hospitals in Missouri have closed in recent years and rural providers face financial stress, there is no reliable evidence that a Missouri rural hospital closes on a strict 'every 8 months' schedule. Also, Missouri voters approved Medicaid expansion by ballot in August 2020 and the program was implemented thereafter, so blaming the legislature's 'failure to expand Medicaid' as stated is misleading without additional context about timing or implementation details.

claim: Says "Joe Biden is absolutely on board with defunding the police."
rationale: Joe Biden has publicly and repeatedly said he does not support 'defunding the police' and campaigned on policing reforms while maintaining funding for law enforcement and community policing. He opposed calls to abolish or fully defund police departments, so the claim that he is "absolutely on board" with defunding is incorrect.

claim: U.S. Rep. Jim Langevin didn't want a border fence to block illegal immigration "because he is afraid that someone will get hurt trying to go around the fence."
rationale: I find no reliable evidence that Rep. Jim Langevin made that specific statement; it appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase taken out of context. While lawmakers, including Democrats, have criticized border fencing on humanitarian and practical grounds, there is no documented quote by Langevin saying he opposed a fence because he was "afraid that someone will get hurt trying to go around the fence."

claim: Says that in three legislative sessions, his proposals opening pre-kindergarten to all Texas 4-year-olds never got heard or voted out of committee.
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because it omits the identity of "his" and the specific sessions or bill numbers; without those details one cannot confirm that proposals to open pre-kindergarten to all Texas 4-year-olds were filed and then never heard or voted out of committee in three sessions. Texas legislative records are public and would be needed to substantiate a claim about a legislator's bills repeatedly dying in committee. Given the missing specifics, the claim is unsubstantiated and judged false for now.

claim: Says "Morgan Carroll opposed requiring convicted sex offenders to register their online profiles, making it harder to track online sex offenders and child predators."
rationale: There is no clear, credible record that Morgan Carroll specifically opposed a law requiring convicted sex offenders to register their online profiles in a way that 'made it harder to track' offenders. Public legislative records and contemporary news coverage of Colorado bills on online identifier requirements do not show her leading or prominently taking that position; some lawmakers expressed constitutional or implementation concerns about particular proposals, which is different from opposing registration per se. The claim appears to conflate procedural or legal concerns with categorical opposition and is therefore misleading.

claim: Says he has "a fiduciary responsibility to his business, his family and his employees to pay no more tax than legally required."
rationale: The claim is presented without attribution or sourcing, so it cannot be verified as a truthful quotation. Without a named speaker or supporting evidence, I cannot confirm that any particular person actually said those words. Because the statement as given is unverified, it should be treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "In 2001 and '02 . . . we had the pension system funded at (the) 100% level in that year, and we did for two years at that point."
rationale: The statement is vague about which pension system it refers to and no widely used pension metric shows general '100% funding' in both 2001 and 2002. Social Security held trust fund reserves after the late-1990s surpluses but was not fully pre-funded to cover all future obligations, and most state and local pension plans were underfunded around that time. Without a specific plan and funding measure, the blanket claim that "the pension system" was 100% funded for two years is not supported.

claim: "Clerks in Milwaukee and Dane Counties colluded to (add) nearly 250,000 individuals to the ‘Indefinitely Confined’ voter list."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that clerks in Milwaukee and Dane Counties colluded to add nearly 250,000 people as 'indefinitely confined.' Wisconsin law and guidance require voters to self-designate or request absentee status, news reporting and post‑election reviews found no proof of coordinated mass additions, and the scale claimed is implausible for just those two counties.

claim: Under H.R. 1, the Federal Election Commission "for the first time ever, instead of being an equal number of Republicans and Democrats (would be) three of one side and two of the other."
rationale: H.R.1 (the For the People Act) proposed changing the FEC’s statutory structure from six commissioners (with a maximum of three from one party) to a five-member commission, which would allow a 3–2 partisan split. Historically the FEC was created as a six-member commission with a 3‑3 partisan limit, so the bill would for the first time create a statutory structure that permits a permanent 3–2 majority.

claim: "The Biden Administration is recklessly releasing hundreds of illegal immigrants who have COVID into Texas communities."
rationale: There is no evidence of an explicit Biden Administration policy to 'recklessly' release hundreds of COVID-positive migrants into Texas communities. Reporting shows isolated instances where overcrowded Border Patrol facilities and humanitarian releases led to some migrants being released and later testing positive, but this is not the same as an organized policy to release hundreds deliberately and without precautions.

claim: Hillary Clinton in 2005 co-sponsored legislation that would jail flag burners.
rationale: There is no clear congressional record showing Senator Hillary Clinton co-sponsored a 2005 bill that would criminalize flag burning and jail flag burners. Public co-sponsorship lists and contemporaneous news/fact-check coverage do not document her as a 2005 co-sponsor of such legislation; the claim likely confuses different proposals or years.

claim: "I've got five years of experience as a national security staffer in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: The statement is a personal employment claim with no supporting evidence provided. Without independent corroboration (named office, dates, or records), it cannot be verified and must be treated as unproven, so I rate it as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "Queen Elizabeth d-e-a-d at age 95."
rationale: The commonly referenced Queen Elizabeth (Elizabeth II) died on 8 September 2022 at age 96, so the claim that she died at 95 is incorrect. The statement misstates her age at death.

claim: Says in the last 20 years, the French have not "stood by" the United States on foreign policy.
rationale: The statement is too sweeping and inaccurate: while France has disagreed with the U.S. on some high-profile issues (e.g., opposing the 2003 Iraq war), it has also actively cooperated with the U.S. in the past 20 years on many major foreign-policy actions. Examples include French participation in NATO operations in Afghanistan, joint action in the 2011 Libya intervention, extensive counterterrorism cooperation, and aligning with U.S. and EU sanctions on Russia. These show France has at times stood with the United States, so the absolute claim that it has not is false.

claim: "The pension fund in the city of Providence is only 30 percent funded, about the same level as when he [Taveras] took office."
rationale: The claim is misleading: Providence's pension funded ratio has been very low but not a stable, exact '30 percent' and funding levels changed during and after Mayor Taveras's term due to policy actions and budgetary changes. Public actuarial reports and contemporary news coverage show funded ratios in the low-to-mid 30s (and varying over time), so stating it is 'only 30 percent, about the same level as when he took office' oversimplifies and misstates the trend.

claim: "We had already issued several thousand Special Immigrant Visas .. to the (Afghan) translators, when I came into office."
rationale: By the time the current administration took office in January 2021, U.S. State Department records and contemporary reporting show that the Special Immigrant Visa (SIV) program for Afghan interpreters had already produced thousands of visas over prior years. The claim’s wording is vague but correctly characterizes that several thousand SIVs had been issued before the speaker assumed office.

claim: Through the Clinton Foundation, "the Clintons are now worth in excess of $100 million."
rationale: The Clinton Foundation is a charitable nonprofit whose assets are designated for charitable programs and not personal enrichment; it did not make the Clintons personally worth over $100 million. While many public estimates place Bill and Hillary Clinton's combined net worth above $100 million, that wealth primarily comes from post-government book deals, speaking fees, and investments rather than foundation funds.

claim: "If I mail in my ballot on Sunday and show up to the polling station on Tuesday, they won’t know if I’ve already voted or not. That, my friends, is a serious concern for all of us."
rationale: Whether poll workers 'know' you already voted depends on the jurisdiction and the status of the mailed ballot; many jurisdictions update voter records when an absentee/mail ballot is received and will prevent or require a provisional in-person vote if a ballot is already returned. If you merely mail a ballot and it has not yet been received or processed, pollworkers may only see that a ballot was issued/requested and may allow an in-person provisional or regular ballot. The blanket claim that they 'won’t know' is therefore incorrect in general.

claim: Jeff Mann has an ethics complaint against him alleging he used county workers for campaign work, which is an indictable offense.
rationale: I could not find verifiable evidence in available sources that a specific ethics complaint alleges Jeff Mann used county workers for campaign work, nor a confirmed determination that such a complaint exists against him. Additionally, whether using county employees for campaign work is an indictable offense depends on the particular state or county law and is not universally an indictable crime.

claim: "I, all the way back in January, warned (President Trump that) this pandemic was coming. I talked about what we needed to do."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific person personally warned President Trump in January and discussed needed actions. Public record shows agencies (CDC, HHS, intelligence) and some officials briefed the administration in January 2020 about COVID-19 risks, but there is no independent, verifiable evidence that the unnamed claimant personally warned Trump in January as described. Without documentary proof (emails, memos, contemporaneous briefings naming the claimant) the individual claim is not substantiated.

claim: Kyle Rittenhouse was an "armed person" crossing state lines when he came to Kenosha protests in 2020.
rationale: Multiple contemporaneous news reports, court testimony, and video evidence show Kyle Rittenhouse traveled from Antioch, Illinois to Kenosha, Wisconsin on August 25, 2020 and was carrying an AR-15–style rifle while at the protests. He was photographed and filmed armed in Kenosha after crossing the state line.

claim: "Embalmers finding ‘strange clots’ in jabbed people"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that embalmers are routinely finding novel or vaccine-specific "strange clots" in people who received COVID-19 vaccines. Medical experts and fact-checkers note that gelatinous clots and postmortem coagulation are common after death and can arise from decomposition, underlying disease, or postmortem changes, and the social-media anecdotes cited have not been verified or linked causally to vaccination.

claim: "There are no provisions in here that substantially affect or advantage the big Wall Street bankers."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim about an unspecified text and cannot be verified as true without knowing which bill or document is meant. Empirically, major legislative or regulatory texts frequently contain provisions that affect large financial institutions and can advantage or disadvantage them, so a blanket claim of 'no provisions' is unlikely. Because the claim is both unverifiable as stated and improbable given historical patterns, I rate it false.

claim: Graduation rates of players at major football colleges "are still twenty points below their male campus peers and worsened in the past three years."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization not supported by available NCAA and federal graduation-rate data. While some football-player cohorts at particular schools have lagged behind their male campus peers, the gap is not uniformly 20 percentage points across major programs, and national aggregated metrics have tended to be stable or improve rather than show a uniform worsening over the past three years. Without a specified metric, set of schools, or precise time window the claim is not supported.

claim: Says "in Oregon today, the average debt upon college graduation is more than $24,000."
rationale: I cannot confirm that Oregon's average debt at college graduation 'today' exceeds $24,000. State-level reports (such as past Institute for College Access & Success analyses) typically show Oregon averages in the low-to-mid $20,000s for recent graduating cohorts, sometimes below $24k, and figures vary by year and methodology. Without a specific current source or year the claim is not reliably supported.

claim: "Germany owes ... vast sums of money to NATO & the United States must be paid more for the powerful, and very expensive, defense it provides to Germany!"
rationale: The claim misstates how NATO and allied financing work: NATO is funded by agreed member contributions and common budgets, not by a system of unilateral 'owed' debts from Germany to NATO. Germany does not owe the United States 'vast sums' as a blanket debt for defense; there are negotiated cost-sharing arrangements (NATO contributions, Germany's defense budget, and host‑nation support for U.S. forces) but no automatic large arrearage requiring the U.S. to be paid more. Political arguments that Germany should increase defense spending are separate from factual claims of an outstanding debt.

claim: Hillary Clinton wants to "wave the white flag of surrender and set a date for withdrawal."
rationale: The claim frames Clinton as advocating 'surrender' and a fixed withdrawal date, which she has not explicitly done. Public statements show she opposed arbitrary timetables (notably in the 2008 campaign) and has supported condition-based or phased drawdowns coordinated with military leaders and allies rather than 'waving the white flag.' The quoted phrase appears to be rhetorical criticism by opponents, not a direct expression of her policy.

claim: Social Security is a "Ponzi scheme."
rationale: Social Security is not a Ponzi scheme because it is a government-run social insurance program funded by payroll taxes and governed by law, not a secret fraudulent operation that deceives investors. While current benefits are paid out largely from current workers' taxes (a pay-as-you-go element), the program is transparent, statutory, and backed by taxing authority and a trust fund, unlike a Ponzi scheme which relies on deception and collapses when new investors stop coming in.

claim: "If Rhode Island does a hybrid [retirement] plan we’ll be the first state in the nation to do this.’’
rationale: Many U.S. states have already implemented hybrid public retirement plans that blend defined-benefit and defined-contribution features, so Rhode Island would not be the nation’s first. Variations in plan design exist, but the general hybrid approach is already in use in multiple states as part of pension reforms.

claim: "Did you know that in 2013 over 50 percent of all babies born in Oregon were Hispanic?"
rationale: State and national birth statistics from that period show Hispanics made up a minority — not a majority — of births in Oregon in 2013. While Hispanic births were proportionally higher than their share of the population in some areas, they did not constitute over 50% of all births statewide.

claim: Says U.S.-Mexico border has "1 million legal border crossings each and every day."
rationale: The claim overstates and mischaracterizes border traffic. Official border-crossing statistics vary by year and category (pedestrians, vehicles, commercial), and annual totals divided by 365 do not support a reliable, constant figure of 1,000,000 legal crossings 'each and every day.' Counts fluctuate seasonally and by port of entry, so the blanket daily claim is inaccurate.

claim: Dan McCready backed state legislation that raised consumers "$149 million a year in higher energy costs."
rationale: I could not find credible evidence that Dan McCready publicly backed any specific state bill that directly resulted in $149 million per year in higher energy costs to consumers. The claim appears to conflate or misattribute a numeric estimate about an energy policy to McCready without identifying a particular enacted law he sponsored or endorsed. Without a clear bill name, vote record, or contemporaneous reporting tying him to that outcome, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Dwayne 'The Rock' (Johnson) Has Officially Filed For The 2020 Presidential Campaign"
rationale: Although Dwayne 'The Rock' Johnson publicly entertained the idea and there was widespread speculation and 'draft' movement enthusiasm, he did not file official candidacy paperwork with the Federal Election Commission for the 2020 presidential election. Major news outlets and FEC records show he never entered the 2020 race.

claim: "Dandelion root is able to kill 98% of cancer cells within 48 hours."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization not supported by clinical evidence. While some laboratory (in vitro) studies have reported that dandelion root extract can kill a high percentage of certain cancer cell lines under controlled conditions, those results are limited to specific cell types, concentrations and experimental setups and have not been shown to translate to humans or to 'kill 98% of cancer cells within 48 hours' broadly.

claim: "Fifteen years ago, you couldn't even get a pizza delivered in that neighborhood."
rationale: The statement is too vague and lacks identifying details to verify; no specific neighborhood, city, or evidence is provided. Pizza delivery availability varies widely by location and over time, so while some neighborhoods may indeed have lacked service 15 years ago, the blanket claim cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: "$53 million a week is coming across the border in drugs."
rationale: The statement is unverified and presented without timeframe, location, or price basis; official seizure reports and expert estimates vary widely and do not support a specific $53 million-per-week figure as a definitive fact. Valuation of drug flows depends on whether wholesale or retail prices are used and seizures undercount total trafficking, so a precise weekly total like $53M is unsupported.

claim: "[Hillary Clinton]'s not trusted -- virtually at all."
rationale: The statement asserts that virtually nobody trusts Hillary Clinton, which is a hyperbolic claim. Repeated national polls and trust/approval surveys over many years show fluctuating but non-negligible percentages of Americans who say they trust or have confidence in her on various issues, so trust is not near zero.

claim: "Our economy is so much stronger than when (Barack Obama and Joe Biden) took office. Nearly 15 million new private-sector jobs."
rationale: The claim that there were "nearly 15 million new private-sector jobs" since Barack Obama and Joe Biden took office is not supported by official payroll data for a clear, stated timeframe. Bureau of Labor Statistics payroll reports show substantial private‑sector job gains over the recovery years, but the commonly cited totals for Obama’s two terms and comparable multi‑year spans are lower than 15 million or depend on choosing specific start/end months to reach that figure. The statement is therefore misleading without a precise timeframe and appears inaccurate as a general claim.

claim: Bernie Sanders has "never taken corporate lobbyist money in his *entire political career.*"
rationale: The absolute claim that Sanders has "never" taken corporate lobbyist money is not supported. While Bernie Sanders has long refused corporate PAC money and publicly rejects lobbyist influence, campaign finance records and news fact-checking note instances where contributions came from corporate-affiliated PACs, corporate employees, or individuals with lobbying ties, so the blanket "never" statement is inaccurate.

claim: Says a video captures sound from the surface of Mars
rationale: NASA's Perseverance rover (and recordings of Ingenuity flights) include microphones that have captured and allowed release of audible recordings from the Martian surface, and NASA has published videos that include those authentic sounds. Thus a video can legitimately contain sound recorded on Mars.

claim: "The Clinton Foundation folded."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the Clinton Foundation has ceased to exist or been dissolved; it continued to operate programs, file nonprofit reports, and maintain a public presence after the period often referenced. Claims that it "folded" likely confuse downsizing, leadership changes, or reduced activity with formal closure. Therefore the assertion that the foundation folded is incorrect.

claim: "CA inmate pregnant after being forced to share prison with transgender ‘woman.’"
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable reporting or official confirmation that a California inmate became pregnant after being forced to share a cell with a transgender woman; similar viral posts have been investigated and debunked by fact-checkers and denials from prison officials. The claim appears to be an unverified social-media rumor rather than a documented incident.

claim: The House budget plan proposes "the largest discretionary spending cut in history."
rationale: The House budget's backers have framed its proposals as the "largest discretionary spending cut in history," but that assertion rests on selective framing (nominal vs. inflation‑adjusted, single year vs. multi‑year, baseline choice). Independent budget analysts and historical data show large prior discretionary reductions depending on how you measure them, so the blanket historical superlative is misleading.

claim: "Since 1999, firearm deaths in Ohio have risen 58 percent."
rationale: The statement is not adequately supported as phrased. Public mortality data (CDC WONDER and state reports) show that the percent change in Ohio firearm deaths since 1999 depends on the end year used and whether one compares raw counts, crude rates, or age-adjusted rates, and none of these standard comparisons cleanly matches a 58% increase without additional context. Because the claim gives no endpoint or measure, it is misleading and cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Mitt Romney did not "endorse" Ted Cruz, even though he said he is voting for Cruz and urged others to do likewise.
rationale: Saying you will vote for a candidate and urging others to do likewise is functionally a public endorsement under ordinary political usage. Even if Romney avoided the specific word 'endorse,' publicly encouraging others to support a candidate constitutes endorsement in common practice.

claim: That Donald Trump said in 1998 if he were to run for president he would run as a Republican because "They’re the dumbest group of voters in the country. They believe anything on Fox News. I could lie and they’d still eat it up. I bet my numbers would be terrific."
rationale: No credible contemporaneous source or reputable fact-checker has been able to verify that Trump made this statement in 1998. The quotation circulates widely online but appears to be a fabrication; Trump's well-documented controversial remarks about voters and media use different wording and come from later years.

claim: Says Donald Trump has outlined "policies that read like a Kremlin wish list."
rationale: This is a subjective characterization rather than an objectively verifiable fact. While some commentators and critics have described certain Trump positions (for example on NATO, sanctions, or comments about Putin) as aligning with Russian preferences, saying his policies 'read like a Kremlin wish list' is interpretive and depends on which policies and who is making the claim. Without attribution and specific policy examples, the statement cannot be treated as a factual claim.

claim: Wisconsin bill "grants drug companies and medical device manufacturers immunity from injuries and deaths caused by their products."
rationale: The statement describes a blanket, absolute immunity. No known Wisconsin bill grants drug and medical device manufacturers unconditional immunity from all injuries and deaths; recent proposals instead offer narrow, conditional liability protections tied to specific circumstances (for example compliance with federal authorization or actions during declared emergencies).

claim: "The reason we even have colleges is that at some point there were politicians who said, ‘You know what? We should start colleges.’ "
rationale: This is an oversimplification: many colleges and universities originated from medieval church institutions, guilds of teachers and students, religious orders, or private philanthropists rather than being created solely because elected politicians decided to start them. While some institutions were later chartered or founded by rulers or governments, it is not accurate to say the reason colleges exist is simply that politicians once said to start them.

claim: "ALERT: Massive Easter Egg Recall Leaves MILLIONS Of Children In Danger- THROW THEM AWAY- They WILL Kill Your Kids."
rationale: The claim is an unsubstantiated, sensational alert with no specific brand, date, or sourcing and no evidence of an authoritative, massive recall that would put millions of children at immediate lethal risk. While toy and candy recalls do occur (often for choking or contamination hazards), official recalls are posted by manufacturers and agencies (CPSC, FDA) and rarely match the hyperbolic language 'will kill your kids.'

claim: Says Thai police found bodies of children with their organs removed.
rationale: There are no credible reports from Thai police, major Thai news organizations, or reputable international outlets confirming that police found children's bodies with organs removed. Similar sensational posts and images have been repeatedly debunked by fact‑checkers as misattributed, out of context, or originating from other countries and incidents.

claim: The Uvalde, Texas, school shooter was a "transsexual leftist illegal alien named Salvatore Ramos."
rationale: The shooter was identified by law enforcement and major news outlets as Salvador Ramos (not 'Salvatore'), an 18-year-old from Uvalde, Texas. There is no credible evidence he was transgender, an 'illegal alien', or a politically motivated 'leftist'—those details were false rumors circulated after the attack.
