rationale: Bureau of Labor Statistics monthly payroll data show that federal government employment rose by roughly 200,000 between early 2009 (when President Obama took office) and early 2011. Most of that increase was driven by temporary hires for the 2010 Census rather than a sustained rise in permanent federal civilian staff.

claim: Says "46 percent of people believe major national news organizations fabricate stories about me."
rationale: The claim asserts a precise 46% figure without naming a source or the person referenced. While reputable polls show large minorities distrust major news organizations and some respondents say outlets sometimes 'fabricate' stories, I am not aware of a credible poll that specifically found '46% of people believe major national news organizations fabricate stories about me' as stated. Absent a cited survey and exact question wording, the statement appears unsupported or misleading.

claim: "Nearly 20% of our residents" are born abroad.
rationale: The claim provides no referent for "our residents" (country, state, or city) or a timeframe, so it cannot be verified as stated. Because the foreign‑born share varies widely by jurisdiction and year—some places are near 20% while others are much lower—the unqualified statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: "President Trump has the strongest support percentage-wise in our state than any other state in the nation. He won West Virginia by almost 43 percentage points and he's been carrying close to 60 percent approval."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate but incomplete facts with a false generalization. Trump did win West Virginia by roughly a 42-point margin in 2016 (often rounded as “about 43 points”), and he is very popular there, but West Virginia is not unambiguously the single state with his highest percentage support — other states (e.g., Wyoming, Oklahoma and some Plains states) have produced equal or higher vote shares for him. Also the statement that he’s been carrying “close to 60 percent approval” in the state is imprecise and depends on timing and poll source; state approval has varied and is not uniformly ~60% across reputable polls.

claim: "Make no mistake -- Sherrod Brown is one of the main D.C. politicians responsible for Ohio jobs moving to China."
rationale: Sherrod Brown is a pro-labor Ohio Democrat who has generally opposed trade deals and criticized offshoring; his voting record and public statements do not support him being responsible for outsourcing jobs to China. Major drivers of Ohio job losses to China were corporate decisions, global supply chains, and trade policy actions such as China's accession to the WTO and broader trade liberalization, not actions by Brown.

claim: "Kids coming from an affluent background" are "taking advantage of all these student loan programs and grants" while many middle-class families with no connection to college are picking up the tab.
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization and conflicts with how aid programs are structured: need‑based grants (like Pell Grants) are targeted to low‑ and moderate‑income students, not the affluent. While federal student loans are broadly available, wealthier students are less likely to receive need‑based grants and overall low‑income students receive a larger share of grant aid; some middle‑class taxpayers do subsidize higher education through federal spending, but it is incorrect to claim affluent kids are universally "taking advantage" of all grants while unrelated middle‑class families are uniformly "picking up the tab."

claim: "We understand that this heroin is primarily coming from Mexico, over the border."
rationale: U.S. federal drug enforcement assessments and seizure data in recent years show that the majority of heroin consumed in the United States is produced in Mexico and trafficked across the U.S.–Mexico border. While other sources (e.g., Colombia or Afghanistan) have supplied heroin historically and regionally, Mexican-sourced black tar and powder heroin dominate most U.S. markets today.

claim: At the State of the Union address, Democrats, "even on positive news … were like death and un-American. Un-American. Somebody said, ‘treasonous.’ I mean, yeah, I guess, why not? Can we call that treason? Why not?"
rationale: This quote matches remarks made by then-President Donald Trump describing Democrats’ reaction to his State of the Union address; he said they looked like “death” and called them “un-American,” adding that someone had said “treasonous” and rhetorically asking if it could be called treason. Contemporary news reports and transcripts of his post–State of the Union remarks record this wording.

claim: Getting the COVID-19 vaccine jeopardizes life insurance policies.
rationale: Life insurance companies do not generally void policies simply because a policyholder received a recommended vaccine such as a COVID-19 vaccine. Insurers base claims decisions on medical cause of death and on whether the policyholder committed material misrepresentation when applying; routine vaccination is not a disqualifying condition in standard policies.

claim: "Obama-Nelson economic record: Job creation ... at slowest post-recession rate since Great Depression."
rationale: The claim overstates the evidence. While job growth after the 2009 recession was unusually slow compared with many post‑World War II recoveries, calling it the "slowest since the Great Depression" is not supported universally — results depend on the exact metric (jobs added, payroll employment, unemployment-rate decline) and the start/end dates used. Fact‑checking and BLS comparisons typically describe the 2009 recovery as one of the weakest postwar recoveries, not uniquely the slowest since the 1930s.

claim: Says North Carolina "hospital beds are typically 85% full across the state."
rationale: Statewide hospital occupancy rates vary over time and are generally lower than a persistent 85% average. Long‑term and pre‑pandemic averages for hospitals nationally and in many states tend to be in the 60–70% range, and while occupancy can spike above 85% during surges, it is not typically that high across North Carolina at all times.

claim: During his time as House speaker, "unemployment came down from 5.6 percent to under 4 (percent)."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous about which 'his' it refers to and does not match available unemployment timelines for recent House speakers. No recent Speaker began their tenure with unemployment at 5.6% and then saw it fall to below 4% purely during their time as Speaker; for example, Paul Ryan became Speaker in late 2015 when unemployment was about 5.0% and unemployment fell below 4% in 2018. Without a specific speaker and dates the claim is not supported.

claim: "It costs more to live in many Florida cities than New York City."
rationale: New York City is widely reported to have higher overall cost-of-living, driven especially by substantially higher housing and transportation costs, than most Florida cities. While certain Florida places (notably parts of Miami or coastal resort areas) can be as expensive or exceed NYC on some specific measures, it is incorrect to say that many Florida cities cost more to live in than New York City overall.

claim: "We've seen in this last year tremendous things happening, including our unemployment rate come down 2 percentage points."
rationale: The claim lacks a specified country and exact 12‑month period, so it cannot be verified as stated. Unemployment can and has moved by about 2 percentage points in some year-long periods for some countries, but without a defined timeframe and jurisdiction the assertion is uncheckable and therefore not reliably true.

claim: Says a "Clorox bottle claimed it could kill (the 2019 coronavirus)... before it was developed."
rationale: This is false as stated. Clorox product labels have long listed efficacy against the category 'human coronavirus' (meaning previously known human coronaviruses), not a specific virus that had not yet emerged; they did not specifically claim to kill SARS‑CoV‑2 before it existed. After SARS‑CoV‑2 appeared, public health agencies noted that products effective against similar coronaviruses should be effective against the new virus.

claim: "Under my administration, 7 million Americans have come off of food stamps, and 10 million people have been lifted off of welfare."
rationale: This claim is misleading and not supported by program data. SNAP (food stamp) participation did decline by several million in the pre-COVID years of the administration, but not clearly by a verifiable net 7 million in the stated timeframe, and the main cash welfare program (TANF) has a caseload measured in the low millions — far below 10 million people — so the assertion that 10 million were 'lifted off welfare' is inaccurate.

claim: In the United States, we’ve had "12 years in a row of wages declining."
rationale: Available US wage data do not show a single 12-year consecutive decline in broad wage measures. Nominal average hourly earnings and median household or median worker incomes have risen in many years, and while some inflation-adjusted (real) measures fell for stretches after the Great Recession, there is no clear 12-year straight decline across standard BLS or Census series.

claim: "More people now die in Wisconsin from drug overdoses than car crashes."
rationale: State and national mortality data in recent years show drug overdose deaths in Wisconsin have risen and surpassed motor-vehicle crash fatalities. Wisconsin Department of Health and CDC reports from the late 2010s through the early 2020s documented more overdose deaths than traffic deaths, largely driven by opioids and fentanyl.

claim: John McCain "began his career in Washington as a lobbyist when he was appointed in 1976 as the Navy's liaison to the United States Senate."
rationale: John McCain did serve as the Navy's liaison to the U.S. Senate in the mid- to late-1970s, but that was as a uniformed naval officer in a government staff/liaison role, not as an outside lobbyist. He was a career Navy officer (and former POW) before that assignment and did not 'begin his career in Washington as a lobbyist.'

claim: Since he took office as Milwaukee County executive, "we have never raised" bus fares and "this year there’ll be a million route-miles more than there were five years ago."
rationale: Publicly available Milwaukee County Transit System (MCTS) records and news reports do not support both parts of this claim. Fare policy and service levels changed during and after the pandemic (including temporary fare suspensions and service adjustments), and MCTS published annual service-mile figures do not show a clear net increase of one million route/service miles compared with five years earlier.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "just gave a speech a few weeks ago" and said "we should still have troops in Iraq."
rationale: I cannot find evidence up to my June 2024 knowledge cutoff that Mitt Romney 'just gave a speech a few weeks ago' in which he said 'we should still have troops in Iraq.' While Romney has historically supported a robust U.S. military presence and criticized rapid withdrawals, the specific recent speech and quoted wording are not corroborated in available records. Without a date or source, the claim as stated is unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: "Exit polls indicate that Democrats get over 70 percent of LGBT votes in federal elections."
rationale: National exit polls and survey data from multiple recent federal elections routinely show LGBTQ voters favor Democratic candidates by large margins, commonly in the roughly 70–80% range. While exact percentages vary by year and poll, the pattern of Democrats receiving over 70% of LGBT votes in many federal contests is well documented.

claim: "Scott Walker has a plan to privatize state lands" and "wants to sell our deer to the highest bidder."
rationale: The statements are hyperbolic and not supported by public records of Scott Walker's policy proposals. While Walker favored some transfers of management authority and budget measures affecting land use, there is no credible evidence he proposed wholesale privatization of state lands or literally selling wild deer to the highest bidder; wildlife in U.S. states is typically managed by state agencies and hunting is regulated via licenses and permits.

claim: "Kids in cages" in border facilities are "at 700% capacity."
rationale: The "700% capacity" claim is a misleading generalization. That figure came from snapshots of specific short-term Border Patrol holding facilities during extreme overcrowding in 2019 and rests on non-standard or disputed definitions of "capacity," not a verified, systemwide occupancy rate for all facilities holding children. Reporters and fact-checkers have noted the number was taken out of context and cannot be applied broadly.

claim: Under Rick Scott, there has been a "historic $20 billion in funds for education."
rationale: The $20 billion figure has been repeatedly promoted by Scott allies but independent fact-checks and budget analyses find it misleading. The number mixes different funding sources, fails to adjust for enrollment growth and inflation, and counts local and federal dollars rather than new state-provided spending, so there is no authoritative basis for a claim that Scott delivered a historic $20 billion in new state education funding.

claim: "Surveys show that many of our citizens think we devote a full quarter or even a third of our federal budget to foreign aid."
rationale: Multiple reputable public-opinion surveys have repeatedly found that many Americans substantially overestimate how much of the federal budget goes to foreign aid, with typical median or mean estimates often in the mid-20s to around 30 percent. Those survey findings contrast with actual federal spending on foreign assistance, which is a very small single-digit share of the budget, so the claim correctly summarizes the survey results.

claim: Says critics who say he cut Medicaid are wrong; his budget added $1.2 billion to the program
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify who “he” is, what jurisdiction or fiscal year is meant, or whether the $1.2 billion is gross, net, or a reallocation. Even if a budget line shows a $1.2 billion increase, that can coexist with policy changes or accounting shifts that reduce services or eligibility, so the blanket rebuttal that critics are “wrong” cannot be confirmed without more context.

claim: Says "FBI and Texas State Police are both confirming that Raymond Peter Littleberry, the man accused of shooting up a Texas church, was an avid atheist on the payroll of the Democrat National Committee."
rationale: There are no credible or official law-enforcement confirmations that link a person named Raymond Peter Littleberry to being an 'avid atheist' on the payroll of the Democratic National Committee in connection with a Texas church shooting. Major news outlets and official FBI/Texas Department of Public Safety press releases typically report verified suspect identities, motives, and employer ties, and this specific set of claims is not corroborated by such sources and appears to be a conflation of unverified allegations.

claim: "Hurricane Irma could be a Category 6 by the time it hits East Coast."
rationale: There is no official 'Category 6' on the Saffir–Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale; it is defined only from Category 1 through Category 5. Even if Hurricane Irma intensified beyond the current highest thresholds, meteorological agencies would still classify it as Category 5 rather than a non-existent Category 6.

claim: "The forest fires were so grotesque last year that we had the worst air in the world in Washington."
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute, but it is ambiguous and not generally true as a sustained fact. While intense wildfire smoke has caused parts of Washington to record some of the worst air quality in the world on certain days (per global AQI trackers), saying "we had the worst air in the world last year" as a blanket statement is unverified and depends on specific dates, dataset, and whether "Washington" means the state or D.C.

claim: Says Gov. Tony Evers "tried to make us pay even more at the pump by hiking the gas tax."
rationale: Governor Tony Evers repeatedly proposed raising Wisconsin's gasoline excise tax (and related vehicle fees) as part of his transportation and budget plans to fund road repairs. Those proposals were reported widely and were framed as increases that would raise pump prices, even though many of his proposals were not enacted as originally written by the legislature.

claim: As Massachusetts governor, Mitt Romney used a line-item veto to cut "millions of dollars for firefighting equipment," including firefighters' "coats, pants, helmets and boots."
rationale: This characterization is misleading. Romney did use line-item vetoes as Massachusetts governor that removed some appropriations labeled for public safety or firefighting equipment, but fact checks found the specifics — that he cut millions directly earmarked for firefighters' coats, pants, helmets and boots — are not supported; amounts, purposes, and outcomes were more complex and some funding was restored or reallocated by the legislature. The claim simplifies and overstates what the vetoes actually did.

claim: Black cats in Vietnam are being killed and consumed as a COVID-19 cure.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Vietnamese authorities or mainstream media reported a widespread practice of killing and consuming black cats as a COVID-19 cure. The claim appears to be a viral rumor; public health organizations and fact-checkers have stated that no animal product is a cure for COVID-19. Isolated acts of animal cruelty, if they occurred, do not substantiate the broad claim.

claim: In Texas, "the No. 1 name for new male babies — many of whom will vote one day — is Jose."
rationale: State-level baby-name data (e.g., Social Security Administration state rankings) show names like Liam and Noah as the top male names in Texas in recent years; Jose does not appear as the No. 1 male name statewide. While Jose is a common name among Hispanic families and may top lists in particular counties or demographic subsets, it is not the overall No. 1 male baby name for Texas in recent SSA data.

claim: "Here are the facts: there is no massive wave of migrants pouring into California. Overall immigrant apprehensions on the border last year were as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years (and 85 percent of the apprehensions occurred outside of California)."
rationale: The claim misstates the data. Official CBP encounter figures for recent years (FY2021–FY2023) show very high numbers — in the millions — not levels “as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years.” While it is correct that the bulk of Southwest Border apprehensions occur outside California (California accounts for a small share), the statement that overall apprehensions last year were near multi‑decade lows is contradicted by CBP annual totals and sector breakdowns.

claim: "In the last several months, the Biden administration has released over 7,000 illegal aliens who were COVID positive just in one Texas city." Biden's border policies are "endangering not just the people of Texas, but people all across the country."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Biden administration released over 7,000 COVID-positive migrants in a single Texas city in the past several months. Public reporting and official CBP and state statements do not corroborate that specific figure, and independent fact-checkers have found such large, city-level tallies unsubstantiated. While migrants have been released under various programs and some tested positive for COVID at times, the precise claim appears to be a misleading exaggeration.

claim: "Before this law was passed, Americans were told they could keep their current health care plans. After it became law, the administration issued regulations stating nearly half of Americans would lose their current plan."
rationale: It is true that President Obama repeatedly said "if you like your plan, you can keep it," and later HHS issued rules on grandfathered plans that meant some noncompliant individual-market policies would end. However, the administration did not issue a regulation saying "nearly half of Americans" would lose their plans — the large losses occurred mainly in the non-group/individual market and the number affected was far smaller than half of all Americans. The claim therefore misstates scope and scale.

claim: Photo shows Barack Obama and George Clooney in a compromising situation with a child.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or major news reporting that Barack Obama and George Clooney were involved in any such incident, and allegations of this gravity about two high-profile public figures would have triggered widespread investigation and reporting. Images of this kind that circulate on social media are frequently manipulated or miscaptioned; absent authoritative sourcing, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: Says Steph Curry decided to split with Nike because the company wouldn’t allow him to write Bible scriptures in his shoes.
rationale: This claim is not supported by the public record. Stephen Curry signed with Under Armour in 2013 rather than having a public ‘split’ from Nike, and there are no credible reports that Nike refused requests from Curry to feature Bible verses; Curry has publicly featured scripture references on his Under Armour shoes with that company’s approval.

claim: "Ohio companies export more goods and services globally than 41 other states."
rationale: The claim lacks a timeframe and appears inconsistent with publicly available U.S. state export rankings. Recent Census-based data on combined goods and services exports generally place Ohio outside the top eight (commonly around 9th–11th), so it does not export more than 41 other states in most recent full-year tallies. Without a specific year or data source the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Colorado school forces students to wear hijabs."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any Colorado public school system has a policy forcing students to wear hijabs. U.S. public schools are prohibited from compelling students to observe religious practices or wear religious garments, and reported stories typically involve voluntary accommodations, private religious schools, or isolated misunderstandings rather than a mandated policy.

claim: Teachers "are working their third consecutive year -- some longer than that -- without salary increases."
rationale: The statement as written implies a broad, ongoing national condition, but teacher pay patterns vary widely by district and state. While some teachers in particular districts have indeed gone multiple years without raises, many other districts and states have implemented pay increases or new contracts in the past three years. Because the claim lacks geographic and temporal specificity, it cannot be supported as a general fact about "teachers" overall.

claim: Says of Gov. Tony Evers and 2020 violence in Kenosha after the police shooting of Jacob Blake: "It took the loss of lives before help finally came."
rationale: Governor Evers ordered state resources into Kenosha before the Aug. 25 shootings: the Wisconsin National Guard and additional state law enforcement were mobilized and deployed on Aug. 24 in response to unrest after the Blake shooting. While some federal assistance arrived later and critics argued responses were slow, it is incorrect to say help arrived only after lives were lost.

claim: Says that in Texas, it’s "already illegal to enter a bathroom to harm someone."
rationale: Texas law already outlaws assault, sexual assault, aggravated assault, criminal trespass, and related offenses, which would make entering a bathroom with intent to harm someone a crime. Those general criminal statutes apply regardless of location, so entering a restroom to injure or sexually assault someone is already illegal.

claim: The polls "show over half of Americans identify themselves as being pro-life."
rationale: Major recent national polls (e.g., Gallup, Pew Research Center, AP-NORC) generally show either a plurality or a majority of Americans identifying as pro-choice rather than pro-life. While some individual polls or particular question wordings can produce >50% identifying as pro-life, the overall polling trend in recent years does not support the blanket claim that polls show over half of Americans identify as pro-life.

claim: Says George Patton said, "Politicians are the lowest form of life on earth. Liberal Democrats are the lower form of politicians."
rationale: There is no reliable primary-source evidence that General George S. Patton ever said this line; the phrase appears to be a later, apocryphal attribution. The wording (particularly 'Liberal Democrats') and lack of appearance in Patton's speeches, writings, or contemporaneous reports make the attribution highly unlikely.

claim: "Only Reuters" reported that the doctor who detected the omicron variant said its symptoms are "very mild."
rationale: This is false. Multiple major news organizations besides Reuters reported that Dr. Angelique Coetzee (the clinician who flagged early Omicron cases) described the cases she saw as mild or "very mild," so Reuters was not the sole reporter of that characterization.

claim: "7 out of 10 Oregon families living in poverty have at least one parent who works."
rationale: I cannot verify the precise claim as stated because it gives no year or data source; while a substantial share of Oregon families in poverty do include at least one working parent, the exact proportion varies by year and definition and is not reliably established as '7 out of 10' without a cited source. Without a specific dataset (e.g., ACS year and family definition) the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Of six Rhode Island tax-credit programs worth about $35 million, "three companies got 90 percent of that -- CVS and two companies not even located in the state of Rhode Island."
rationale: I could not verify the specific claim that three companies (CVS plus two out-of-state firms) received 90% of roughly $35 million across six Rhode Island tax-credit programs. CVS is headquartered in Rhode Island, and allocations of state tax credits are published in official reports; the claim is specific but uncited and appears inconsistent with available public reporting practices. Without named programs, a timeframe, or supporting state data, the assertion is not substantiated.

claim: Says Aaron Rodgers "is not the highest tax rate payer" in Wisconsin, it's "the single mom getting 24 grand in benefits with two kids who will lose 80 cents on the dollar if she goes and takes a job."
rationale: The claim overstates and conflates two different concepts. Wisconsin has progressive statutory income tax rates that apply highest rates to top earners (which would include high-paid professionals), whereas low-income households can face high effective marginal tax rates when means‑tested benefits are withdrawn; that effect can be substantial but depends on which benefits are counted. There is no general, documented fact that a generic single mom receiving $24,000/year in benefits in Wisconsin would automatically ‘lose 80 cents on the dollar’ if she takes a job, so the specific numeric assertion is unsupported.

claim: "The U.S. spends more money on its military than the 16 biggest military budgets in the world" combined.
rationale: The U.S. defense budget (roughly $800–900 billion in recent years) is larger than any other single country and has exceeded the next ~10 countries combined in some years, but the combined totals of the next 16 largest military spenders (China, Russia, India, UK, Saudi Arabia, Germany, France, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Italy, Brazil, Israel, Canada, Spain, Netherlands, etc.) exceed the U.S. total. Summing typical recent budget estimates for those 16 countries yields a figure above the U.S. budget, so the claim that the U.S. spends more than those 16 combined is not correct.

claim: "Flip Flop! After opposing term limits for decades, Adam Putnam adopts Donald Trump and Ron DeSantis’ position."
rationale: The claim alleges a long-standing opposition by Adam Putnam to term limits and a recent switch to adopt Donald Trump and Ron DeSantis’ position, but I find no clear public record showing decades of opposition followed by a definitive adoption of a specific Trump/DeSantis term‑limits stance. Putnam has not been widely documented as a major national voice on the specific presidential or congressional term‑limit proposals associated with Trump or DeSantis, making the broad claim unsupported. Without precise timelines or which term‑limits are meant, the assertion overstates available evidence.

claim: Proposition 2 on November’s Texas ballot "does not cost state taxpayers any money."
rationale: A blanket claim that Proposition 2 "does not cost state taxpayers any money" is misleading. Texas constitutional amendments are accompanied by Legislative Budget Board fiscal notes and many measures that claim no direct cost still create implementation, enforcement, or litigation expenses for state agencies or local governments. Without specifying the year and reading the official fiscal analysis, the zero-cost assertion is not reliably supported.

claim: RNC version of a Hillary Clinton valentine: "Roses are red, violets are blue, I'll raise your taxes and there is nothing you can do."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the Republican National Committee officially produced or distributed a valentine with that exact wording. The rhyme appears to be a partisan meme or parody that circulated on social media and has been attributed to various GOP sources without verification. Political groups sometimes create satirical valentines, but this specific quote is not documented as an RNC-issued statement.

claim: "A Florida judge ruled parts of Obamacare unconstitutional."
rationale: In January 2011 U.S. District Judge Roger Vinson in Florida ruled that the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate was unconstitutional and concluded the law could not stand. That decision was appealed and the Supreme Court later upheld key parts of the law in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012).

claim: "Ten retired nuns were barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary."
rationale: Contemporary reporting on the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary described an incident in which about ten retired nuns at a care facility were initially turned away or faced confusion at the polls, but they were not permanently prevented from voting; election officials intervened and the situation was resolved. Thus the claim that ten retired nuns 'were barred from voting' as a final outcome is misleading.

claim: "Biden says he doesn’t need voters to get elected."
rationale: There is no reliable record of President Biden flatly saying he does not need voters to get elected; clips that circulate claiming this are edited or taken out of context. In full remarks Biden has typically urged people to vote or made rhetorical distinctions (e.g., addressing donors or emphasizing he wants rather than 'needs' votes), so the absolute claim is misleading.

claim: Says Rick Scott "didn’t even come to his own education summit. But he did take time to go to the tea party convention the same week."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it gives no date, location, or source for which "education summit" and which "tea party convention" are meant. Public schedules, press releases, and news coverage are required to confirm whether Rick Scott missed a specific summit while attending a Tea Party event in the same week, and no definitive corroborating evidence was identified without that context. Given the missing specifics, the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false for now.

claim: Ninety percent of the job growth in Virginia has been in the private sector.
rationale: The statement is presented without a timeframe or source and therefore cannot be verified as a general fact. Official employment statistics (BLS and Virginia Employment Commission) show that the share of job growth in the private sector varies by period and is not universally 90%; such high percentages are sometimes true for specific, short windows but not as a blanket claim.

claim: "My opponent, in 2008, had contributions investigated by the federal government."
rationale: The claim is presented without naming the alleged opponent or specifying what "contributions" refers to, so it cannot be verified as stated. Confirming that federal authorities investigated someone’s contributions in 2008 requires identifying the person and referencing DOJ, FEC, or contemporaneous news records; none are provided. Absent those specifics the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The majority of my contributions have been from private individuals" giving $125 on average, "not from PACs, not from groups."
rationale: The claim gives specific summary statistics (majority from private individuals, $125 average, not from PACs/groups) but provides no candidate, time period, or supporting data. Campaign finance assertions require examination of official filings (e.g., FEC or state reports) to verify sources and average donation amounts; without those records the specific numeric claim cannot be substantiated. Because the statement is unverified as presented, it is treated as false.

claim: "Individuals and small businesses will be hit by increases in health insurance premiums as high as 39 percent."
rationale: The claim is an unqualified blanket statement with no timeframe, location, or policy context; premium changes depend heavily on the specific law, year, market, and individual circumstances. While some analyses of particular proposals or markets have shown very large increases for certain groups, there is no general, verifiable finding that individuals and small businesses broadly will be hit with increases “as high as 39 percent.”

claim: Says Kurt Schrader voted to cut $500 billion from Medicare, threatening "thousands of Oregon seniors and their access to their current coverage."
rationale: There is no clear record that Rep. Kurt Schrader voted for a bill explicitly cutting Medicare by $500 billion; as a Democrat he generally opposed major Republican proposals that would have reduced Medicare benefits. Ads claiming he voted to cut $500 billion appear to conflate complex budget scoring, proposed policy changes, or other members' votes with his record. Without a specific bill and vote showing Schrader supporting a $500 billion direct cut to Medicare, the claim is misleading and not supported by clear evidence.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "wants higher standards for toy guns than real guns."
rationale: There is no credible record of Bernie Sanders saying he 'wants higher standards for toy guns than real guns.' Sanders' public statements and policy positions consistently call for stricter regulation of real firearms (background checks, assault-weapons limits), not looser standards for them relative to toys. The claim appears to be a misquote, satire, or out-of-context distortion.

claim: "Obama administration kept illegal Mexican kids in detention camps as ‘experiment’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Obama administration deliberately kept undocumented Mexican children in detention camps as an 'experiment.' While the Obama era did use family and child detention facilities and implemented deterrence-focused immigration enforcement that critics condemned, characterizing those practices as a deliberate experimental program is unsupported by official records or reputable reporting.

claim: "The pope and Donald Trump and Tammy Baldwin all agree" on eliminating the "carried-interest" tax break.
rationale: Tammy Baldwin has explicitly supported legislation to end the carried-interest tax preference and Donald Trump at times said during his campaign he would eliminate or change the carried-interest treatment. Pope Francis has repeatedly condemned inequality and tax avoidance, but there is no clear authoritative record of the pope specifically calling for elimination of the carried-interest tax break as a tax-policy prescription. Because the pope's statements are moral critiques rather than explicit endorsements of that specific U.S. tax change, the claim that all three 'agree' is not supported.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Duffy is among seven "Tea Party freshmen" who "spent an average of $15,000 on cars for themselves."
rationale: I cannot find reliable evidence that Rep. Sean Duffy was one of seven Tea Party freshmen who personally spent an average of $15,000 on cars; the claim is vague about source, timeframe, and whether amounts were campaign expenditures or personal purchases. Similar circulated claims have tended to conflate legitimate campaign vehicle expenses or reimbursements with personal spending, making the allegation misleading. Without clear documentation tying Duffy to such a list and amount, the assertion is not supported.

claim: "We do not have an overcrowding problem. As a matter of fact, Rhode Island has one of the lowest incarceration rates in the country."
rationale: The blanket statement denying any overcrowding is misleading; although Rhode Island typically ranks among the states with lower per-capita incarceration rates, that does not preclude facility- or county-level crowding or temporal spikes. National corrections data generally place Rhode Island in the lower tier for incarceration rate, but local jail/prison capacity and recent trends determine overcrowding and can differ from the statewide rate.

claim: The EPA "wants to hire 230,000 new government regulators that will cost the taxpayer $21 billion."
rationale: The claim is not supported by available facts: the EPA’s total workforce is on the order of tens of thousands (roughly ~14,000 employees), not 230,000 new hires, and there is no credible proposal from the agency to hire 230,000 'regulators.' The $21 billion figure appears to be a mischaracterization or conflation of cost estimates from regulatory analyses and compliance costs over time, not a line-item cost for hiring 230,000 new government employees.

claim: Says in "our region," 2011 was worst drought year ever recorded.
rationale: The statement is too general and cannot be validated because 'our region' is unspecified; drought severity is measured regionally and 2011 was the worst year on record in some places (e.g., parts of the United States and East Africa) but not universally. Without a defined region and supporting local hydrological records, the claim that 2011 was the worst drought 'ever recorded' for an unspecified region is unsubstantiated.

claim: If you paid rent in March or April, "they got to give" you your money back.
rationale: There is no universal rule that rent paid in March or April must be returned. Whether tenants are entitled to refunds depends on the specific lease, local or state laws, and any emergency relief or rent-abatement programs in effect at the time; some jurisdictions provided relief during COVID-19, but refunds were not automatic everywhere.

claim: "If there is a firearm available, it is 17 times more likely to be used either for suicide or for assaulting a friend, relative, an acquaintance than it is to be used in fending off an intruder."
rationale: There is no widely accepted, robust evidence that a firearm being available makes it 17 times more likely to be used for suicide or assault of acquaintances than for fending off an intruder. Epidemiological studies do show that guns in the home are associated with higher risks of suicide and homicide, and estimates of defensive gun use vary widely and are contested, so a precise 17× multiplier is not supported as a general fact.

claim: "People are less likely to just vote for party now. … They’re looking at the personalities."
rationale: Broad empirical evidence from recent decades indicates party identification and partisan voting have generally strengthened, with increased straight-ticket and polarized voting in many democracies; this contradicts the claim that people are now less likely to vote on party. While candidate personality can influence some swing voters and individual races, the dominant trend in political science is toward stronger party influence, not weaker.

claim: Says New Jersey has "the highest unemployment rate in the region" and "stagnant job growth."
rationale: The claim is vague and therefore not reliably true: it does not specify the time period or what geographic "region" is being referenced, and New Jersey has not consistently had the highest unemployment nor uniformly "stagnant" job growth compared with neighboring states. Labor force and payroll data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and state labor departments show unemployment rates and job growth rates vary month-to-month and year-to-year, so the assertion cannot be verified as a general fact without a specific timeframe and comparator set.

claim: "Obama has proposed 442 tax hikes since taking office."
rationale: Independent fact-checkers have found the "442" figure is an inflated tally that mixes duplicate line items, fee changes, and various budget proposals rather than 442 distinct, enacted tax rate increases proposed by President Obama. While Obama proposed some tax increases (notably targeted at high earners) in his budgets, the methodology behind the 442 number is misleading and does not represent 442 separate tax hikes.

claim: Says John F. Kennedy "smoked cannabis in the White House, while president, because he suffered from severe back pain and Addison's disease."
rationale: There is no credible historical evidence that John F. Kennedy smoked cannabis in the White House while president. JFK's chronic, severe back pain and extensive prescription drug treatments (painkillers, steroids, amphetamines, sedatives) are well documented in biographies and medical histories, but marijuana use is not supported by reliable primary records or mainstream scholarship.

claim: Miami-Dade County is the "No. 1 donor county in the state."
rationale: The claim is overly general and lacks a timeframe or definition of "donor" (total dollars, number of contributors, or per-capita). Miami-Dade is Florida's largest county and often ranks near the top for political contributions, but rankings change by election cycle and by metric, so it is not universally the "No. 1 donor county in the state."

claim: "I've created over 40,000 jobs."
rationale: The claim as presented is missing a named subject, time period, geographic scope, and whether ‘created’ means direct hires, indirect jobs, or cumulative over time. Without those specifics or supporting payroll or official employment data, the statement cannot be substantiated and is therefore treated as false in this context.

claim: "Under Rick Scott, homeowners are paying higher (home insurance) premiums for less coverage."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization and asserts a direct causal link to Rick Scott that is not fully supported. Florida homeowners did see premium increases in the 2010s and some policies shifted to higher deductibles or fewer options, but those changes were driven by multiple factors (storm losses, reinsurance costs, insurer market exits) and coverage reductions were not uniform statewide or solely attributable to Scott's actions.

claim: "Lauren Boebert received a PPP loan for her restaurant."
rationale: Contemporaneous news reports and publicly released PPP loan data show that Shooters Grill, the restaurant owned/operated by Lauren Boebert and her husband, received a Paycheck Protection Program loan in 2020. Boebert has also acknowledged that the restaurant obtained pandemic relief funds.

claim: Tide gauges measuring sea level in Rhode Island since 1930 have risen "maybe about 10 inches since that time."
rationale: Tide-gauge records for Rhode Island (Providence/Narragansett area) show roughly 2.5–3.5 mm per year of relative sea-level rise over much of the 20th century, which accumulates to about 8–12 inches from 1930 to today. Saying 'maybe about 10 inches' is a reasonable summary of those measured trends, though exact values depend on the station and exact time window.

claim: "I got a letter from 20 people who said they wanted their money back, 14 never gave me a penny."
rationale: The statement is a specific, self‑reported anecdote (a count of 20 letter writers and that 14 never gave money) for which there is no publicly available evidence or documentation to confirm. Without primary documents, names, or independent reporting corroborating the numbers, the claim cannot be verified and should be treated as unproven. Because this is an unverifiable personal anecdote rather than a documented fact, I classify it as false for purposes of fact-checking.

claim: "From 1990 to 2015 under (Democratic) control, W. Va. teacher pay rank plummeted from 30th in the nation to 48th."
rationale: Published teacher-salary ranking tables do show West Virginia slipping in rank over time, but the precise claim that it was 30th in 1990 and 48th in 2015 is not corroborated by standard NCES/NEA historical tables—early-1990s ranks differ by source and 2015 rankings vary by measure. The statement also implies a causal link to continuous "Democratic control," which is a vague attribution not supported by the salary data alone.

claim: "We’re at the point of reaching 2 million deportations ... this is a historic level, more than any other president of the United States."
rationale: Historic DHS enforcement data show prior presidents—most notably Barack Obama—oversaw more than 2 million formal removals during his two terms, so reaching 2 million now would not be "more than any other president." The claim also conflates different measures (removals, returns, expulsions) that change the totals and comparisons.

claim: The man in a mugshot is "responsible for lighting 32 of the wildfires" on the West Coast.
rationale: There are no credible, corroborated law-enforcement or news reports identifying a single individual in a widely circulated mugshot as having started 32 separate West Coast wildfires. Wildfire causes are usually attributed to lightning, utility equipment, accidents, or isolated arson incidents, and a mass-arson arrest of that scale would be widely documented; the claim lacks those verifications.

claim: "Coroner saying George Floyd died of drug overdose, not police brutality."
rationale: The Hennepin County Medical Examiner's autopsy determined George Floyd's death was a homicide due to cardiopulmonary arrest complicating law enforcement subdual, restraint, and neck compression. Although toxicology detected fentanyl and methamphetamine, the coroner did not attribute the death solely to a drug overdose, so the claim that the coroner said he died of overdose rather than police brutality is incorrect.

claim: "When they say Mexico can't pay for the wall, I say of course they can. We have a trade deficit with Mexico that's unbelievably big. ... It's billions and billions of dollars -- far more than what we're talking about for the wall."
rationale: It is true the U.S. has run a sizeable bilateral trade deficit with Mexico in recent years (tens of billions annually), which can exceed some estimates of the wall's cost. However, the claim that this means "of course" Mexico can pay for the wall is misleading: the trade deficit reflects private cross‑border trade flows and corporate/household payments, not a pool of Mexican government funds that can be used to pay U.S. government construction costs.

claim: Marijuana today is "genetically modified," with THC levels that "far surpass the marijuana" of the 1970s.
rationale: The statement is misleading: while THC concentrations in cannabis have increased substantially since the 1970s (typical averages rose from roughly 1–3% then to commonly 10–20% or higher in modern samples), most of that change comes from selective breeding, cloning and cultivation practices (e.g., sinsemilla), not from genetic engineering or transgenic modification. Saying marijuana today is “genetically modified” implies laboratory genetic engineering, which is not the norm in commercial cannabis production.

claim: Says Donald Trump's claim that "there was insufficient evidence and therefore, in our country, a person is innocent" directly contradicts Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s statement.
rationale: Mueller explicitly said his investigation did not exonerate the president and that "if we had confidence that the president clearly did not commit a crime, we would have said that." Trump's assertion that "insufficient evidence... therefore... a person is innocent" conflicts with Mueller's statement that the report did not clear the president. Thus the two statements are directly at odds on whether lack of charges or conclusive evidence equals exoneration.

claim: Military spending cuts, known as the sequester, were President Barack Obama’s idea.
rationale: The 2013 sequester grew out of the Budget Control Act of 2011, a bipartisan deal reached during debt-limit negotiations in which automatic, across-the-board cuts were written into law as a fallback enforcement mechanism. It was not a unilateral proposal by President Obama; the mechanism was negotiated with congressional leaders and the law preserved sequestration as a joint congressional–executive compromise. The general idea of sequestration as a budget tool also predates Obama.

claim: Says five studies show his tax plan can cut rates and still bring the same revenue without raising taxes on the middle class.
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as written: no publicly verified set of five studies is widely accepted to show that an unnamed politician’s tax plan can cut rates while keeping total revenue unchanged and without raising middle‑class taxes. Independent nonpartisan scorekeepers and mainstream economic analyses typically find that large rate cuts reduce revenue unless they rely on strong, contested dynamic‑growth assumptions or unspecified offsets. Without identification of the plan and the five studies and their methods, the claim is not supported.

claim: The federal health care law raises taxes and cuts Medicare.
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included new revenue provisions (for example, an additional 0.9% Medicare payroll tax on high earners and a 3.8% net investment income tax) that raised taxes for higher-income individuals, and it also reduced Medicare spending growth by cutting payments to Medicare Advantage plans and trimming certain provider and hospital payments. Those Medicare payment reductions were used in part to finance coverage expansions and deficit reduction rather than to cut beneficiary benefits directly.

claim: "We have one of the lowest mortality rates in the world" from COVID-19.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable and misleading as written because it does not identify who "we" refers to nor which mortality measure (case fatality rate, infection fatality rate, or deaths per capita) or time period is meant. International COVID-19 mortality rankings vary over time and by metric, so a blanket claim without those specifics cannot be supported and is likely false or at best ambiguous.

claim: "Sixty percent of New Jersey doctors do not accept Medicaid patients."
rationale: Available state and national physician-survey data and reports from Medicaid programs indicate that a majority of New Jersey physicians accept Medicaid patients; the proportion refusing Medicaid is substantially lower than 60%. Acceptance rates vary by specialty and by whether physicians are taking new Medicaid patients, so a blanket 60% refusal figure is not supported by typical evidence.

claim: "Masks will kill quite a few people, it’s well known that they reduce blood oxygen levels and those with respiratory and cardiac disorders will die."
rationale: This claim is false. Numerous clinical studies and guidance from public-health agencies show that cloth and surgical masks do not meaningfully reduce blood oxygen or raise CO2 for the vast majority of people, and there is no evidence that routine mask use is causing deaths. People with severe, unstable respiratory failure may find masks uncomfortable and should seek medical advice, but that does not validate the broad assertion that masks "will kill quite a few people."

claim: More than 500,000 mail in ballots in Virginia and 200,000 in Nevada were sent to dead people or pets
rationale: State election officials and multiple independent fact-checkers investigated these claims and found no evidence that hundreds of thousands of mail-in ballots were sent to dead people or pets in Virginia or Nevada. Confirmed errors and anomalous registrations exist but are very small in number and often result from outdated rolls, mailings of absentee ballot applications (not completed ballots), or clerical issues — nowhere near the 500,000/200,000 totals. The claim conflates different kinds of mailings and inflates isolated anomalies.

claim: Says the "South African Government is now seizing land from white farmers" and alleges a "large scale killing of farmers" in the country.
rationale: While the South African government has debated and pursued legal changes to enable land expropriation without compensation as part of land reform, it has not been conducting widespread, systematic seizures of land from white farmers. Likewise, violent attacks on some farmers have occurred, but independent data and official crime statistics do not support a coordinated, large-scale campaign of killing farmers or a genocide against white farmers.

claim: "There have been some estimates that if you deported everybody who is in Texas illegally," it "would create an economic recession for the state."
rationale: Multiple economic analyses and policy reports have modeled the impact of removing undocumented immigrants from Texas and found large GDP, employment, and tax-revenue losses; some of those estimates explicitly warned that mass deportation could be severe enough to trigger a recession in the state under certain assumptions. The claim only asserts that 'some estimates' reach that conclusion, which is supported by existing studies and reports.

claim: Says there’s "no wait list" for private school vouchers
rationale: As a blanket statement it is inaccurate: private school voucher programs are administered by states or districts and often have funding limits or enrollment caps that create wait lists. While a particular program at a particular time might have no wait list, claiming universally that there is "no wait list" is misleading without naming the program and date.

claim: "If we went back to the obesity rates that existed back in the 1980s, the Medicare system over several years could save as much as a trillion dollars."
rationale: Credible health-economics estimates find obesity raises Medicare and overall health spending substantially, but they generally put Medicare-attributable savings from returning to 1980s obesity levels in the hundreds of billions over long time horizons, not a clear "trillion dollars over several years." There is no consensus or peer-reviewed estimate showing Medicare alone would save as much as $1 trillion in just a few years under realistic assumptions.

claim: "In this country, we have a 25 percent dropout rate."
rationale: The claim is unspecified and unverifiable as stated because it does not name the country, the education level (primary, secondary, tertiary), the timeframe, or the metric (annual vs. cohort dropout rate). Dropout rates vary widely by country and by definition, so a blanket statement of '25 percent' requires a cited statistic from a reliable source. Without that context or evidence the assertion should be treated as false.

claim: Coca-Cola, Ben & Jerry’s and other companies support rioting.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Coca‑Cola, Ben & Jerry’s, or major mainstream companies officially endorse or encourage rioting (violent, illegal acts). Many corporations have issued statements supporting racial justice or peaceful protest, made donations to community groups, or criticized violence; that is not the same as supporting rioting. Accusations that companies 'support rioting' typically conflate corporate statements about social issues with endorsement of violence.

claim: Only "18 percent of jobs are accessible by transit for metro Atlanta residents. 33 percent for those living in the city."
rationale: The quoted percentages appear in some transit studies but only under a specific methodology (typically jobs reachable within a set travel-time, e.g., 45 minutes) and for a particular year and geographic definition. Presented without that context the statement is misleading: such figures can be roughly in that range for certain measures, but they are not universally true for all definitions of "accessible by transit" or all timeframes.

claim: "The first (state) budget that came out of our Republican leadership slashed funding to Planned Parenthood...It resulted in the reduction of hours, the elimination of days, elimination of access to women in my city and all over my state."
rationale: The claim does not identify the state or year and cannot be independently verified as stated. While Republican-led state budgets have in some cases reduced funding to Planned Parenthood and those cuts have sometimes led to reduced clinic hours or closures, the specific causal assertion here lacks the necessary state-specific budget documents or local reporting to confirm it.

claim: "Barbara Buono by the numbers: As a Trenton politician, she voted to raise taxes 154 times. Under her, property taxes up 70 percent. Backed a 16 percent sales tax increase. Utilities, nursing homes, cell phones, parking lots, lottery wins, gyms – She taxed them all. Architect of Corzine’s budget, she drove New Jersey $2 billion into debt. Barbara Buono by the numbers: taking New Jersey backwards."
rationale: The statement bundles several true elements (Buono was a long‑time New Jersey state senator and chaired the Senate Budget Committee during the Corzine years, and the 2009 budget raised the sales tax by one percentage point) with exaggerated or unsubstantiated numeric claims and causal attributions. Specifics such as "voted to raise taxes 154 times," "property taxes up 70 percent under her," and "drove New Jersey $2 billion into debt" are presented without context or clear, verifiable methodology and therefore are misleading. While parts of the ad echo real budget actions, the sweeping, precise totals and sole blame placed on Buono do not hold up to scrutiny.

claim: "This is the slowest job recovery since Hoover."
rationale: Using the standard jobs metric (total nonfarm payrolls or employment peak-to-peak), the recovery from the 2007–2009 recession took longer to regain pre-recession employment levels than any postwar recovery and is generally characterized as the slowest recovery since the Great Depression/Hoover era. While other measures (like the unemployment rate or labor-force participation) can show different patterns, the commonly cited jobs-recovery comparison supports this statement.

claim: "Hidden" in the healthcare.gov code is language that means users "waive any reasonable right to privacy of your personal information."
rationale: The token 'Hidden' in website source code is generally a technical/display attribute (HTML/CSS) and is not legal language that can by itself cause users to waive privacy rights. Healthcare.gov's public privacy policy does not contain a clause stating users 'waive any reasonable right to privacy of your personal information,' and legally enforceable waivers require clear, explicit consent and proper notice. A stray label or code comment cannot create a binding legal waiver.

claim: Quotes Winston Churchill as saying "Diplomacy is the art of telling people to go to hell in such a way that they ask for directions."
rationale: There is no reliable primary-source evidence (speeches, writings, or contemporaneous reports) that Churchill said this, and serious quote-researchers have found earlier or unattributed printed variants predating common attributions to Churchill. The line is widely misattributed to him in later sources rather than documented in his own corpus.

claim: "Interior deportations under Obama were down 40 percent and at a nine-year low."
rationale: The statement is misleading: DHS/ICE statistics show removals peaked around FY2012 and later fell, but whether 'interior deportations' were down exactly 40% and at a nine-year low depends on the precise metric and baseline year. Public reports use different measures (total removals, interior removals, apprehensions) and no authoritative source supports that blanket phrasing for the entire Obama presidency without additional context.

claim: A Marine painted his house red, white and blue after he "was told by his neighbors that he could not fly the American flag in his yard all year long."
rationale: I cannot find corroborating, verifiable reporting of a specific Marine who painted his entire house red, white and blue in direct response to neighbors telling him he could not fly the American flag year‑round. The claim resembles a viral anecdote that lacks named parties, location, or reputable news coverage, which reduces its credibility. Without independent sources confirming the incident, it should be treated as unverified and likely false.

claim: "We're No. 46 out of 50 states... we're 46th in terms of percentage of deaths in nursing homes."
rationale: The claim as written is not verifiable because it does not identify which state, which time period, or which data source is being used for the ranking. Rankings of the percentage of deaths occurring in nursing homes vary substantially by dataset (state reports, CDC, KFF) and over time, so a blanket statement that 'we're 46th out of 50' cannot be confirmed without those specifics.

claim: Says Joe Biden stayed silent about violence at Black Lives Matter protests.
rationale: This claim is inaccurate as a general statement: Joe Biden publicly addressed the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests multiple times and explicitly condemned violence and looting while urging peaceful protest and calling for policing reforms. Although critics argued he did not always use particular labels (e.g., 'Antifa') or respond instantly to every incident, he did not remain silent about violence associated with BLM demonstrations.

claim: Says Jeb Bush "said he would take his pants off and moon everybody ... Nobody reports that."
rationale: There is no credible record or news reporting that Jeb Bush ever said he would 'take his pants off and moon everybody.' A remark this sensational would very likely have been widely reported and archived in public transcripts, video, or news coverage, but no such evidence is available. The wording appears to be either a misattribution, a joke, or a fabricated quote.

claim: Hillary Clinton "has already said she's going to wipe out the Second Amendment. She doesn't believe in the First Amendment. And, she also believes in big government, which flies in the face of the 10th Amendment"
rationale: There is no record of Hillary Clinton saying she would ‘wipe out the Second Amendment’—she has publicly supported gun-control measures, not repealing the amendment. Likewise, she has not said she rejects the First Amendment; she has defended free-speech principles while supporting certain campaign-finance and harassment policy changes. The claim’s third clause (that she "believes in big government" and thus violates the 10th Amendment) is a political interpretation rather than a factual quote and is therefore misleading as presented.

claim: "There’s more murders with hammers last year than...shotguns and pistols and AK-47s."
rationale: Available national homicide statistics show firearms — especially handguns/pistols — account for the majority of murders, while killings by blunt objects (the category that would include hammers) are a small minority. Assault rifles like AK-pattern weapons are uncommon but combined with pistols and shotguns still exceed murders specifically committed with hammers in recent annual U.S. reports.

claim: "Court orders Obama to pay $400 million in restitution."
rationale: There is no credible record or major news reporting that any court has ordered Barack Obama to pay $400 million in restitution. Such a significant legal judgment against a former U.S. president would be widely reported and is not present in legal databases or mainstream media. The claim appears to be fabricated or a misattribution.

claim: "KXL Radio in Portland reported today that Firefighters are now being shot at by suspected Antifa and BLM members."
rationale: There is no reliable, corroborated evidence that KXL in Portland reported firefighters are being shot at by suspected Antifa and BLM members. Claims of that nature would almost certainly be documented by the radio station itself, local police/fire authorities, and multiple reputable news outlets; the absence of such corroboration makes the specific assertion unsupported and likely false or a misattribution.

claim: Aaron Bean voted to give illegal immigrants in-state tuition.
rationale: There is no clear public record that Aaron Bean voted to grant in-state tuition specifically to undocumented (illegal) immigrants. Bean is a Republican whose legislative record does not show support for measures broadly described as giving in-state tuition to unauthorized immigrants; claims like this typically stem from mischaracterized votes or confusion about bills with more limited residency or merit provisions. Without citation of a specific bill and roll-call showing he voted that way, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "More businesses are closing than opening in Virginia today."
rationale: The claim makes a definitive, day-specific statement for which no real-time public dataset exists; openings and closures are reported in periodic statistics (monthly/quarterly) and vary by sector and county. Without contemporaneous, authoritative data for Virginia on that specific day, the claim cannot be verified and should be rejected. Even official sources that track business births and deaths report with a lag, so a blanket 'more are closing than opening today' is unsupported.

claim: "Years of economic decay are over" because Trump "reversed the failed economic policies of the previous administration."
rationale: The United States did not experience 'years of economic decay' immediately prior to Trump's term; the post-2009 recovery produced sustained GDP growth, falling unemployment, and job gains. While the Trump administration enacted tax cuts and deregulatory measures that coincided with some short-term gains, economists say attributing an end to an alleged multiyear 'decay' solely to reversing prior policies is unsupported and overlooks other factors and mixed longer-term effects.

claim: "We have the lowest corporate tax rate since 1968."
rationale: The U.S. federal statutory corporate rate was cut to 21% by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (effective 2018). While 21% is the lowest federal statutory rate in many decades, historical tax tables and contemporary fact-checks indicate the statement is misleading without context (some accounts describe it as the lowest in roughly 80 years), and the phrase “since 1968” is imprecise and can be false depending on whether one means federal vs. combined (federal+state) or statutory vs. effective rates. Because the claim offers no context, it cannot be taken as an accurate, unqualified historical claim.

claim: Says Missouri Democratic Senate candidate Jason Kander is "attending fancy dinners all over the country."
rationale: The phrase is a vague, subjective accusation and is not supported by specific, verifiable evidence. While Jason Kander did make national appearances and engage in fundraising during his Senate campaign, there is no documented proof that he was routinely "attending fancy dinners all over the country" as an established pattern rather than occasional fundraising or speaking events.

claim: "324,000 pregnant people experience domestic violence during their pregnancy."
rationale: The claim is presented without timeframe or geography and is therefore misleading. A frequently cited estimate of about 324,000 pregnant women refers to an older U.S. annual estimate of intimate partner violence from national survey data, not a current, global, or context-free fact.

claim: "If you’re a single mom, and you’ve two kids in the city of Richmond, you can almost make $50,000 a year on the public dole."
rationale: The statement is an exaggeration and lacks specification of which programs or year are being counted. Typical cash welfare (TANF) is small, SNAP provides modest food assistance, and most large supports (Medicaid, housing vouchers) are non-cash benefits or reduce expenses rather than provide income, so combining realistic benefit amounts rarely approaches $50,000/year for a single mother with two children in a U.S. city.

claim: Says Florida Gov. Rick Scott "just signed a bill that could make most of Florida’s beaches private."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Gov. Rick Scott signed a law that would convert most of Florida's beaches into private property. Florida's public trust doctrine and long-standing legal protections preserve public access to the wet-sand beach, and past legislation typically made limited changes affecting property rights or beach maintenance rather than wholesale privatization.

claim: Says Bruce Braley took "tens of thousands from his friends in the health insurance industry" and gave them "special favors" by voting for Obamacare.
rationale: Braley did vote for the Affordable Care Act, but there is no credible evidence that he accepted 'tens of thousands' specifically from health insurance companies and then granted them illegal 'special favors.' Campaign contribution records show routine donations from various industries and no documented quid‑pro‑quo tied to his ACA vote. The claim mixes a true fact (his vote for Obamacare) with an unproven insinuation of corrupt exchange.

claim: "Disease-ridden" migrants from parts of Africa with Ebola are being "dumped in San Antonio."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that migrants carrying Ebola have been intentionally 'dumped' in San Antonio. Ebola outbreaks are rare, would trigger public-health notifications, and U.S. border and local health authorities conduct screening and monitoring; no federal or Texas health agency or reputable news outlet has reported such an incident. The claim appears to be an unsubstantiated rumor or misinformation.

claim: Hillary Clinton advocates "a freeze on foreclosures. Barack Obama said no."
rationale: During the 2008 Democratic primary and the early stages of the financial crisis, Hillary Clinton publicly called for a temporary moratorium or freeze on certain foreclosures to protect homeowners. Barack Obama opposed a broad, blanket moratorium and instead promoted targeted relief and market-based solutions, so characterization that Clinton advocated a freeze and Obama said no is accurate.

claim: "We are almost halfway to our goal of 1,000 rapes prosecuted!"
rationale: The claim provides no jurisdiction, timeframe, or source and therefore cannot be corroborated. Counts of criminal prosecutions are public records tracked by specific agencies; without identifying who "we" refers to or citing official data, the statement is unverifiable and should be treated as false until supported.

claim: Says opponent Ted Cruz has not led businesses.
rationale: Public biographical records show Ted Cruz's career has been as a lawyer, Texas solicitor general, and U.S. senator rather than as the founder or CEO of private companies. He is not known to have held executive roles running commercial businesses commonly described as 'leading businesses.'

claim: When he was Milwaukee County executive, "eight years in a row we pushed through budgets that did not increase the tax levy from the previous year."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Public fact-checks and budget records show the claim depends on a narrow accounting definition and omission of one-time fixes, fee increases and other revenue shifts; at least some budget years and different measures of county taxes did rise during his tenure. Saying simply “eight years in a row we pushed through budgets that did not increase the tax levy” therefore overstates the straightforward truth.

claim: Says 2010 was the "worst year ever for America's doctors" reimbursed by Medicare.
rationale: There is no objective evidence that 2010 was unambiguously the "worst year ever" for physicians paid by Medicare. Medicare payment history includes many years with large cuts, freezes, or threats (for example SGR-related cuts in earlier decades and other years with real declines in physician Medicare income), and the label "worst ever" is subjective and depends on which metric is used.

claim: A Fox News affiliate reported on a shooting before it happened.
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify and there is no specific, widely documented instance showing a Fox News affiliate definitively reported a shooting before it occurred. While news organizations sometimes publish erroneous or premature reports, claiming this happened requires a date, location, or verifiable clip to substantiate.

claim: "When Rachel Zenzinger was on the Arvada City Council, she voted to spend taxpayer funds for a junket to China."
rationale: I found no clear, corroborated evidence that Rachel Zenzinger cast a council vote authorizing city taxpayer funds specifically for a “junket to China.” The claim appears in partisan attacks but public reporting and available summaries do not document a definitive Arvada City Council vote funding a leisure trip; details cited in attacks often lack supporting municipal-record citations or conflate sponsored delegations with city-funded travel.

claim: The administration has issued rules for "$1 abortions in ObamaCare" and "requires all persons enrolled in insurance plans that include elective abortion coverage to pay" an abortion premium.
rationale: The Department of Health and Human Services issued rules requiring insurers that offer plans with elective abortion coverage to collect and segregate a separate abortion premium from enrollees, and some exchange plans set that separate surcharge as low as $1 per month. Thus the administration's rules enabled the widely reported “$1” abortion surcharge and required enrollees in plans that include elective abortion coverage to pay the separate premium.

claim: Bill McCollum "backed Jim Greer's effort to hide financial irregularities."
rationale: Jim Greer, former Florida Republican Party chairman, was convicted of financial misconduct and later made allegations about party leaders, but there is no credible, corroborated evidence that Bill McCollum 'backed' any effort by Greer to hide financial irregularities. McCollum has denied such involvement and no courts or reputable investigations have substantiated that claim.

claim: Says the Georgia Dome would need up to $350 million in work over the next five to seven years.
rationale: I cannot verify a specific authoritative statement that the Georgia Dome would need up to $350 million in work over the next five to seven years. While public debate before the Dome's replacement included multi-hundred-million-dollar renovation estimates, figures varied by source and no single verified claim matching this exact phrasing is confirmed.

claim: "BREAKING: Trump family donates $1 billion to wall fund."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official announcement that any member of the Trump family donated $1 billion to a wall fund. Known private wall fundraisers (e.g., “We Build the Wall”) collected far smaller sums and were widely covered and scrutinized; a billion-dollar family donation would have generated prominent, verifiable coverage and legal/financial filings. The claim appears fabricated or misleading.

claim: Before "our last three presidents, you have to go back to the 1800s, early 1800s to find three presidents in a row being consecutively re-elected."
rationale: This is false because there is a clear recent sequence of three consecutive presidents who were each re-elected: Bill Clinton (re-elected 1996), George W. Bush (re-elected 2004), and Barack Obama (re-elected 2012). Therefore you do not need to go back to the early 1800s to find three presidents in a row who won re-election.

claim: Says Conor Lamb "ran on a campaign that said very nice things about me."
rationale: The claim as given is ambiguous and unattributed—there is no identified speaker or evidence showing Conor Lamb ran a campaign that explicitly "said very nice things about me." Without a named subject or a specific quoted campaign statement, the assertion cannot be verified. Public records of Lamb's campaigns do not support an undifferentiated claim that his messaging universally praised an unnamed individual.

claim: Delaware has the "eighth-largest black population in the country"
rationale: Interpreted in the usual way (absolute number of Black residents), Delaware does not have the eighth-largest Black population — many much larger states have far greater Black populations by raw count. Even if the claim meant share (percentage of state population), Delaware does not consistently rank eighth among states in Black population percentage according to recent U.S. Census data.

claim: "The child tax credit, if we don't do it, there will be no tax relief for working families. How much tax relief working families get under tax reform is entirely dependent on whether or not we put in place an increase to the child tax credit."
rationale: The statement is incorrect as an absolute claim. Tax relief for working families can come from multiple provisions — e.g., lower tax rates, a higher standard deduction, expansion of the Earned Income Tax Credit, or payroll tax changes — not solely from an increase in the child tax credit. While enlarging the child tax credit would increase relief for many families, it is not the only mechanism that determines whether working families receive tax relief.

claim: Says the logo of a porn website appeared during a CNN broadcast.
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable reporting that a porn website logo actually appeared during a CNN broadcast; similar images have circulated on social media as doctored screenshots and hoaxes. Major news outlets and fact-checkers typically report and correct such incidents, and no such widely corroborated incident involving CNN has been documented.

claim: Says Ayn Rand said, "The question isn’t who is going to let me; it’s who is going to stop me."
rationale: The line is widely attributed to Ayn Rand online, but there is no reliable primary-source citation in her published books, essays, or verified speeches that confirms she wrote or said it. Quote-tracking research and scholarly bibliographies of Rand do not substantiate the attribution, so the claim is likely incorrect.

claim: Says Betsy Devos said "only" 0.02% of kids are likely to die when they go back to school.
rationale: The claim is misleading.
