rationale: Typical household spending data show housing (mortgage or rent) is the single largest expense for most U.S. households, while out‑of‑pocket health care spending is substantially smaller on average. Although some individuals or families—particularly the elderly or those with major chronic illnesses—can face medical bills that exceed their housing costs, it is not true broadly that health care costs now exceed mortgage or rent 'in many instances' across the population, nor is this a unique first in American history.

claim: "Corporate entities are paying a lot less taxes this year than they have in the past. Part of that is from a loophole in a bill that was passed in 2015."
rationale: The claim is misleading and likely incorrect: the major, widely cited U.S. corporate tax change was the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (rate cut from 35% to 21%), not a 2015 bill, and whether corporations pay "a lot less" in any given year depends on profits, deductions, and timing of receipts rather than a single 2015 "loophole." There is no clear evidence that a 2015 law created a broad loophole causing a sharp, generalized drop in corporate taxes this year.

claim: "Not a single person in the crowd on January 6 was found to be carrying a firearm. Not one."
rationale: Multiple law-enforcement reports and Department of Justice charging documents show that some people connected to the Jan 6 events were found in possession of firearms or charged with weapons offenses (including firearms found in vehicles associated with attendees), so the absolute claim that not a single person was carrying a firearm is incorrect.

claim: Congressman Robert Hurt has a plan to cut education by 40 percent.
rationale: There is no documented, specific policy authored by Congressman Robert Hurt that is a public 'plan to cut education by 40 percent.' This claim appears to be a broad or misleading characterization; while Hurt supported budget measures that reduced federal education spending in some years, asserting a standalone 40% cut as his plan lacks verifiable sourcing and context.

claim: Under President Barack Obama: 4 million jobs lost, unemployment rose from 7.8% to 9.9%, the S&P 500 was 1,115.1 and the GDP went down 2.8%.
rationale: The claim mixes and misstates figures and timeframes. Over the full Obama presidency (2009–2017) the U.S. economy added roughly 11–12 million net payroll jobs (not a 4 million loss); unemployment did rise early after he took office (about 7.8% in Jan 2009 to a peak ~10% in late 2009) but then fell to about 4.7% by his departure; the S&P 500 value cited (1,115.1) does not match the index level at inauguration or at term end and appears taken out of context; real GDP did contract in 2009 but the annual decline was about -2.5%, not exactly -2.8% as stated.

claim: "92 percent" of President Barack Obama's administration has "never worked outside government."
rationale: The 92% figure is not supported by reliable counts and has been debunked by multiple fact-checkers. It stems from a narrow or misleading classification of who counts as part of the 'administration' and ignores many appointees with prior private-sector, legal, business, or academic jobs. Broader tallies show a much larger share had experience outside government.

claim: "SpongeBob’s license address is Jeffrey Epstein’s private island!"
rationale: SpongeBob is a fictional character whose onscreen license and addresses refer to locations in the fictional Bikini Bottom (commonly shown as 124 Conch Street), not a real-world private island. Jeffrey Epstein’s private island was a real place (Little St. James in the U.S. Virgin Islands) and there is no credible evidence linking it to any SpongeBob prop or licensing detail. The claim appears to stem from a meme or doctored image rather than factual connection.

claim: "Disney stock is down more than 70% and attendance is down more than 55%! 10.1 million people canceled their Disney+ subscription."
rationale: The claim bundles several metrics without a timeframe and gives numbers that do not match available company and market data. Disney's share price has not declined by more than 70% from recent multi-year peaks in the periods commonly cited, park attendance recovered substantially after the pandemic and is not down by 55% relative to typical pre-COVID levels, and Disney+ has seen churn and some quarterly subscriber declines but not an immediate 10.1 million cancellations reported in a single disclosed period. These specific round figures are therefore misleading or incorrect as stated.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccine could lead to prion diseases, Alzheimer’s, ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that COVID-19 vaccines cause prion diseases, Alzheimer’s, ALS, or other neurodegenerative diseases. Proposed mechanisms (such as mRNA inducing prion formation or altering DNA) are inconsistent with how mRNA vaccines work and have not been supported by laboratory, clinical, or epidemiological data. Large-scale safety monitoring and peer-reviewed studies have not detected an increase in neurodegenerative disease incidence attributable to vaccination.

claim: Says President Obama has cracked down "on employers who are attracting undocumented immigrants and hiring them more than any previous president."
rationale: The statement is a broad comparative claim that lacks supporting evidence. While the Obama administration did increase certain workplace enforcement actions and conducted high-profile raids, there is no clear, authoritative metric showing it cracked down on employers more than every prior president; employer enforcement dates back to the 1986 IRCA and varied across administrations. Because the claim asserts an absolute "more than any previous president" without specifying the measure, it is not supported.

claim: Says his GOP challenger, Doug MacGinnitie, "hadn’t voted in a Republican primary for almost 20 years until 2008.
rationale: I cannot find verifiable, public evidence confirming that Doug MacGinnitie refrained from voting in Republican primaries for nearly 20 years until 2008. Voting-history assertions require inspection of official state voter records or credible contemporary reporting, which are not available to confirm this specific gap. Because the claim is specific and lacks corroboration, it should not be treated as established fact.

claim: Stay-at-home orders "actually are the law of these states."
rationale: The statement is misleading because stay‑at‑home orders are typically executive or public‑health orders issued under governors' or health agencies' emergency powers, not legislative statutes passed by state legislatures. Those orders can have the force of law while in effect in many states, but authority and enforceability vary by state and some orders were subject to successful legal challenges. Without specifying which states or what is meant by "the law," the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We must block Trump from stopping the return of the heroic Alabama mother from ISIS. In many ways she is more of a hero then our veterans. Welcome home sister!"
rationale: There is no credible record of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez saying or tweeting this quote; major fact-checkers and searches of her official statements and social media show the quote is fabricated and has been circulated as a misattribution. The wording and context match viral misinformation patterns rather than any documented AOC statement about an Alabama woman who joined ISIS.

claim: West Virginia has "the nation’s lowest workforce participation rate, which hovers around 50 percent, when the national average is about 63 percent."
rationale: West Virginia does have one of the country’s lowest labor-force participation rates, but recent annual BLS figures put it in the low-to-mid 50 percent range rather than “hovering around 50 percent.” The national civilian labor force participation rate is indeed about 62–63 percent, so the national comparison is roughly correct but the specific West Virginia figure stated is understated.

claim: "Of those 850,000 (new Texas) jobs, most were public-sector jobs and minimum-wage jobs."
rationale: Available labor data show that the vast majority of net job gains in Texas have been in the private sector (leisure & hospitality, trade, construction, professional services, education/health), not public-sector jobs. While many new positions in sectors like hospitality are low‑paid, there is no evidence that most of 850,000 net new jobs were government positions or paid at the minimum wage; public employment is a relatively small share of total payrolls.

claim: "Only the fully vaccinated should fear the new ‘worst ever’ Covid-19 variant; data shows they already account for 4 in every 5 Covid deaths"
rationale: The claim is misleading: vaccines substantially reduce risk of severe disease and death, and reports that a large share of deaths occurred in vaccinated people can arise when most people (especially the elderly) are vaccinated — a base‑rate effect — or when waning/booster status and comorbidities are not accounted for. There is no general evidence that only the fully vaccinated should fear a new variant, nor unambiguous support for the blanket statement that vaccinated people already make up 4/5 of COVID deaths without precise context (time, place, age groups, and booster definitions).

claim: Says 89 members of Congress "hold dual citizenship with Israel."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official list that 89 sitting members of the U.S. Congress hold Israeli citizenship. Publicly available biographies, disclosures, and prior fact-checks show only a very small number of U.S. politicians have any documented Israeli citizenship or were born in Israel, and the large figure appears to originate from viral, unverified claims.

claim: "As your Lieutenant Governor…I cut your taxes."
rationale: Framed as a personal accomplishment, the claim implies the lieutenant governor individually 'cut your taxes.' In nearly all U.S. states tax changes require legislative action (and typically the governor's approval), and the lieutenant governor rarely has unilateral authority to enact tax cuts. Without naming the state or specific legislation, the statement is misleading and cannot be verified as a factual unilateral action by a lieutenant governor.

claim: "Most of your serial killers, most of your people who commit domestic violence, they start off by abusing animals."
rationale: The statement overgeneralizes. While animal cruelty is associated with some violent offenders and is a component of older hypotheses like the Macdonald triad, empirical research does not support that a majority of serial killers or most domestic violence perpetrators began by abusing animals; rates vary and many do not have documented histories of animal abuse. Co-occurrence between pet abuse and intimate partner violence exists, but it is not a universal or reliably antecedent pattern for most offenders.

claim: "Biden's plan is a 14% tax hike on middle class families."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: Biden's major tax proposals generally target corporations and higher-income households (top marginal rates, capital gains for high earners, etc.), not a uniform 14% tax hike on middle-class families. Independent analyses of his proposals do not show a 14% increase in taxes for middle-income households; many middle-income households would see little change or targeted benefits rather than that kind of across-the-board increase.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Casten has held numerous "invite-only" town halls.
rationale: Available reporting and public schedules of Rep. Sean Casten show he has regularly held public or virtual town halls and constituent meetings; while he has occasionally taken smaller donor or constituent calls, there is not clear evidence that he has routinely held numerous strictly "invite-only" town halls. The claim overgeneralizes isolated or informal private calls into a broad pattern.

claim: Says that under President Donald Trump, "not only have we not gone after al-Qaida ... our president is supporting al-Qaida."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Trump or his administration directly supported al-Qaida. The U.S. under Trump continued counterterrorism operations and strikes against al-Qaida and its affiliates, though some policy choices (e.g., troop withdrawals and the Syria pullback) were criticized as creating conditions that could indirectly benefit extremist groups. Describing those indirect effects as the president "supporting" al-Qaida is a misleading characterization.

claim: "More people without health care since George Bush took office; more children in poverty since George Bush took office."
rationale: U.S. government data and independent analyses show that during George W. Bush's presidency the number of uninsured Americans rose and the number and rate of children in poverty increased compared with when he took office. Both trends are documented in Census Bureau and national health statistics for the 2000s.

claim: "Chinese lunar rover finds no evidence of American moon landings."
rationale: Chinese lunar rovers (e.g., Yutu and Yutu-2) have operated in locations that are not the Apollo landing sites and have not reported a systematic search for or definitive absence of American artifacts. Independent evidence for Apollo hardware on the Moon exists from high-resolution lunar orbiter imagery (showing landers, rover tracks, and retroreflectors) and has not been contradicted by Chinese missions. A failure to observe Apollo gear from a different landing site is not the same as proving there is no evidence.

claim: Republicans included "the Akin amendment in the Republican Party platform, which bans abortion, even for rape victims."
rationale: Todd Akin did propose an amendment to the 2012 Republican platform to remove rape/incest exceptions, but his amendment was rejected by the platform committee and was not included in the final Republican Party platform. Therefore Republicans did not adopt an "Akin amendment" that bans abortion even for rape victims as part of the party platform.

claim: "68% error rate in Michigan Voting Machines. Should be, by law, a tiny percentage of one percent."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Michigan voting machines have a 68% error rate; official certifications, logic-and-accuracy testing, and post-election audits are designed to ensure very low error rates and publicly reported audits and certifications do not show anything like 68% machine failure. The 68% figure appears to come from misinterpreted data or small-sample artifacts rather than a statewide error rate, and while law and standards require high accuracy and audit procedures, there is not a universal statutory threshold phrased as 'a tiny percentage of one percent.'

claim: "The states that have raised the minimum wage (this year) have had faster job growth than the states that haven’t raised the minimum wage."
rationale: The statement is presented as a blanket fact but is ambiguous and unsupported without specifying the year and providing state-by-state data. Empirical evidence on minimum-wage increases and job growth is mixed, and observed faster growth in some raising states can reflect other factors (economic cycle, industry mix, selection bias) rather than causal effects of the wage change. Therefore the claim cannot be affirmed as generally true.

claim: Say a "left wing extremist, chases down, rams car over Trump bumper sticker."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific criminal act by a politically labeled individual but provides no sourcing, time, location, or identifying details. Without corroboration from reliable news reports, police records, or video evidence, the allegation cannot be verified and should be treated as false.

claim: Emails show that Fauci knew "hydroxychloroquine worked [and] emailed friends about it being effective."
rationale: Released FOIA emails do not show Dr. Anthony Fauci telling friends that hydroxychloroquine definitively "worked." The emails include forwarded articles, anecdotal comments, and calls for proper clinical trials, and Fauci repeatedly expressed that evidence was mixed or lacking rather than endorsing HCQ as effective.

claim: Says Keanu Reeves gave a speech that began, "I cannot be part of a world where men dress their wives as prostitutes by showing everything that should be cherished ..."
rationale: There is no credible record or primary source showing Keanu Reeves gave a speech beginning with that line; the wording appears on social media and quotation sites as a viral, misattributed quote. Searches of news archives, interviews, and documented public statements by Reeves do not contain this phrasing, so the attribution is unsupported.

claim: In President Barack Obama’s 2015 State of the Union address, "the words ‘al-Qaida’ were never used, the first time those words have not been used in a State of the Union address since February 2001."
rationale: The claim is not correct. The assertion that 2015 was the first State of the Union since February 2001 not to use the words 'al-Qaida' is inaccurate because usage and spelling of the name varied across SOTU transcripts and some earlier addresses also did not use that exact form; fact-checks and comparisons of official SOTU transcripts show the statement is misleading. The hyphenation/spacing ('al-Qaida' vs 'al Qaeda' or 'al-Qaeda') and possessive forms further make the claim unreliable as stated.

claim: "The soda tax can make a difference by reducing consumption of unhealthy soda pop and sugary beverages."
rationale: Multiple empirical studies and natural experiments show that taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages tend to reduce purchases and consumption by raising retail prices. Examples include measurable declines after Mexico's national tax and local U.S. taxes (e.g., Berkeley), though the size of the effect varies by tax level, pass-through, and consumer responses.

claim: The federal government "has $3 trillion in cash flow, so we can pay our bills" and won’t default.
rationale: The claim is misleading: while the federal government does collect trillions in annual receipts, it does not carry a ready $3 trillion cash balance and cannot simply ignore the statutory debt limit. Incoming cash receipts are timing-dependent and may not cover near-term obligations, and legal borrowing constraints or timing mismatches could still force a default on some payments.

claim: The Murray-Ryan deal "is the first divided-government budget agreement since 1986."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because there were bipartisan budget agreements under divided government after 1986. Notable examples include the 1990 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act under President George H.W. Bush and the 1997 Balanced Budget Agreement reached during the Clinton years with a Republican Congress, so the Murray-Ryan deal was not the first since 1986.

claim: Says "taxes were raised 115 times in the eight years before I became governor" and those increases were part of a "path that led to wealth and jobs and people leaving our state."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented: saying 'taxes were raised 115 times in the eight years before I became governor' depends entirely on definitions (state vs. local taxes, fee increases, budgeting actions) and no specific state or timeframe is given. The causal claim that those increases produced a 'path that led to wealth and jobs and people leaving our state' is speculative and unsupported without rigorous economic and migration analysis; multiple factors drive wealth, jobs, and migration.

claim: "In 2009, Yost spent 2.5 times more money than it took to run the (prosecutor’s) office before he got there."
rationale: I cannot verify the claim as stated: it names only 'Yost' and gives no source or detailed budget figures. Claims that an official 'spent 2.5 times more money than it took to run the office before he got there' require specific pre/post budget numbers and accounting categories; without those I find the assertion unsubstantiated. Absent clear, sourced budget comparisons for the named person and office in 2009, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: Says that "18 children died while in custody of Border Patrol" during the Obama administration.
rationale: Claims that 18 children died while in U.S. Border Patrol custody during the Obama administration are unsupported by available records and contemporary fact-checking. Public CBP custodial-death records and independent fact-checkers found no evidence of 18 child deaths in Border Patrol custody in that period; some cited deaths involved other agencies, occurred outside the stated timeframe, or involved children who died after release.

claim: Says Adam Putnam "was for amnesty."
rationale: The claim as stated is misleading. Adam Putnam has repeatedly opposed a broad, blanket "amnesty" for undocumented immigrants and emphasized enforcement and border security, though he has supported limited, conditional relief for Dreamers rather than open-ended amnesty. Without a cited source or a definition of "amnesty," labeling him as "for amnesty" misrepresents his record.

claim: Federal regulations required the changes to Georgia's driver’s license renewal process.
rationale: There is no single federal regulation that directly mandates a state's detailed driver’s license renewal procedures. Federal law (notably the REAL ID Act) sets minimum identity/documents standards for licenses used for federal purposes, which can force states to collect additional documentation, but states retain broad discretion over renewal processes and Georgia’s specific procedural changes were state policy choices to implement or comply with requirements rather than a direct federal mandate of the exact renewal steps.

claim: "To give a sense of how families are struggling, a record four out of every 10 school kids in Ohio now qualifies for subsidized lunch."
rationale: The statement presents a specific, time‑bound numeric record but I cannot verify that exactly 40% of Ohio students currently qualify nor that this is an all‑time record. Official counts of free and reduced‑price meal eligibility fluctuate by year and depend on whether 'subsidized' means only free meals or both free and reduced; without a date or data source the claim is unsubstantiated and likely misleading.

claim: Sen. Mark Kelly voted "for benefits to illegals."
rationale: The statement is a vague, inflammatory paraphrase with no specific bill or roll-call attached; there is no clear record of Sen. Mark Kelly voting in a way that can be accurately summarized as a blanket vote "for benefits to illegals." Kelly has voted for some immigration-related and humanitarian measures that provide limited services to migrants, but those are specific policy votes, not a single broad authorization of benefits to undocumented people. Without a named vote or bill, the claim is misleading.

claim: Rhode Island's state pension system "underperformed the median three out of the four years that Mr. [Frank] Caprio was in office."
rationale: The statement is misleading because yearly ranking of Rhode Island’s pension returns depends heavily on the chosen comparison group, exact fiscal-year definitions, and whether returns are net of fees. Publicly available pension-return datasets and prior evaluations show that when standard benchmarks and consistent fiscal-year definitions are used, Rhode Island’s system was not clearly below the median in three of the four years Caprio held office. Without a specified median benchmark and precise years, the claim cannot be substantiated as stated.

claim: The Senate Republican education plan is an unfunded mandate for local school districts.
rationale: The claim is too general and cannot be verified without identifying a specific Senate Republican education plan and examining its statutory language and funding provisions. Different GOP education proposals vary—some include federal funding or flexible block grants, while others alter responsibilities—so it is incorrect to assert universally that a Senate Republican plan is an unfunded mandate. Absent a named bill or text showing a federal requirement imposed on local districts with no accompanying funding, the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: "750 days since Bill Nelson & the Democrats in the Senate passed a budget. How can this be justified?"
rationale: The claim is incorrect because Bill Nelson has not been a U.S. Senator since January 2019 (he later became NASA Administrator in 2021), so he and 'the Democrats in the Senate' cannot be credited with passing a recent Senate budget 750 days ago. Additionally, federal budgets require action by both the House and Senate and usually the president’s signature, so attributing a budget solely to Nelson and Senate Democrats is misleading.

claim: Fewer Democrats were on the Georgia general election ballot in 2012 than in more than 100 years.
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and ambiguous — there is no clear evidence that the 2012 Georgia general election ballot contained the fewest Democratic candidates in over a century. Democrats continued to appear on numerous 2012 general-election contests (U.S. House, state legislative and other offices), and historical comparisons require a defined metric (statewide contests vs total candidates) which the claim does not provide. Given the lack of specific supporting data and the implausibility of a 100+ year low across all ballots, the statement is not supported.

claim: Says that PolitiFact Ohio confirms that Betty Sutton "maxed out federal debt"
rationale: There is no clear record that PolitiFact Ohio 'confirmed' a claim that Betty Sutton literally 'maxed out federal debt.' PolitiFact typically evaluates specific statements and assigns a rating; available summaries and recollections of fact-checks do not show an endorsement of that exact phrasing and instead treated such language as partisan rhetoric to be rated on its specifics.

claim: "We just don't want to get to be like Louisiana, where you have drive-up daiquiri shops."
rationale: Drive-up/drive-through daiquiri shops are a well-documented and distinctive feature in parts of Louisiana (notably the New Orleans area and other Gulf Coast communities). Numerous news reports and local ordinances have discussed and regulated these establishments, confirming their existence.

claim: "Barack Hussein Obama will ... force local authorities to allow Occupy protesters to live in parks."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Barack Obama announced or enacted a plan to force local authorities to permit Occupy protesters to live in local parks. The President’s authority to override local ordinances is limited, and actions of that kind would typically require specific federal jurisdiction or court orders, neither of which were reported. Assertions that he would compel all local governments to allow encampments misstate the scope of executive power.

claim: Says the state’s budget shortfall is "not that much different" than it was in 2003.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated and is likely misleading because it gives no state or metric; state budget shortfalls vary widely and must be compared in inflation‑adjusted dollars and using consistent accounting. Fiscal conditions in 2003 differed from other years (notably after the 2008–09 recession), so a blanket statement that a state's shortfall is "not that much different" from 2003 is implausible without specific, comparable figures.

claim: The "top ten most unhealthy U.S. cities" are San Francisco; Seattle; Portland, Oregon; San Diego; Honolulu; Washington; Austin, Texas; Irving, Texas; Portland, Maine; and Denver.
rationale: This list is incorrect: the named cities (San Francisco, Seattle, Portland OR/ME, San Diego, Honolulu, Washington, Austin, Irving, Denver) are commonly ranked among the healthiest U.S. cities in typical public-health and quality-of-life surveys, not the most unhealthy. Independent rankings of "most unhealthy" cities usually feature many smaller or economically distressed cities in the South and Midwest with high rates of obesity, smoking, and chronic disease. No reputable recent list identifies this set of largely West Coast and affluent cities as the top ten unhealthiest.

claim: "Suntrust Bank cancels account because company sells guns."
rationale: The claim is presented without specifics and there is no clear, widely reported evidence that SunTrust systematically cancels accounts solely because a company sells lawful firearms. Banks sometimes close accounts for regulatory, risk, or policy reasons, but attributing a cancellation specifically to gun sales requires a verifiable cited incident. Without a specific case, date, or corroborating reporting, the claim is not supported.

claim: Two federal government buses "stopped in front of a Mexican restaurant in the very small town of Green Cove Springs Florida… The passengers were illegal immigrants, straight from the southern border."
rationale: There is no verifiable, widely reported evidence that federal buses dropped off migrants in front of a Mexican restaurant in Green Cove Springs as described. Federal agencies typically transport migrants to processing facilities, and claims identifying people as 'illegal immigrants, straight from the southern border' require documentary confirmation that is not provided here.

claim: Barack Obama is the "First President to terminate America’s ability to put a man in space."
rationale: Calling Barack Obama the "first" president to terminate America's ability to put a person in space is incorrect. The U.S. has had earlier periods without domestic crewed launches (for example, after Apollo-Soyuz in 1975 there were no U.S. crewed launches until the Shuttle began in 1981), and program cancellations and retirements that removed domestic launch capability involved decisions made under Nixon/Ford/Carter and later under George W. Bush as well. Obama did oversee the retirement of the Space Shuttle in 2011 and relied on Soyuz and later commercial crew to restore U.S. launches, but he was not the first president to preside over a loss of domestic crew-launch capability.

claim: Says the Obama Administration has fulfilled all of Texas’ requests for fire management assisting grants.
rationale: Federal fire management assistance grants are approved case-by-case by FEMA based on specific criteria, and historically not every state request is approved. Records and reporting from the Obama years show some wildfire and fire management requests were denied or only partially funded, so the blanket claim that the Obama Administration fulfilled all of Texas’s requests is incorrect.

claim: "FREE HORSES!!!! 52 thoroughbred horses need homes. Will go to Sugarcreek this Sat. for slaughter. Gentleman died due to COVID-19 and his son wants nothing to do with them."
rationale: This reads like a viral, unverified social-media plea and there are no corroborating reports from local news outlets, animal welfare organizations, or government animal control that would normally document the disposition of that many thoroughbreds. Posts claiming large numbers of animals 'free' and 'going to slaughter' are a common format for scams or misinformation seeking attention or contact details.

claim: Dozens of artists, including Justin Timberlake, Jay Z and Rihanna, are canceling Florida shows like Stevie Wonder in protest of  "stand your ground."
rationale: There is no evidence that “dozens” of major artists canceled Florida shows in protest of Stand Your Ground, and the high-profile names listed (Justin Timberlake, Jay‑Z, Rihanna) did not publicly cancel Florida dates for that reason. While a small number of performers (for example Stevie Wonder) publicly criticized the law or pulled a Florida date at one time, widespread mass cancellations by many top artists did not occur as claimed.

claim: The stimulus bill "promised to keep unemployment under 8%."
rationale: No major federal stimulus bill contains a literal, enforceable promise to keep the national unemployment rate below 8%. At times politicians and administration officials have made optimistic projections or claims that a package would limit unemployment, but those are forecasts or political statements rather than a binding promise written into the legislation.

claim: Says Miami-Dade Mayor Carlos Gimenez "approved a 67% pay raise for himself and increased his own pension. He makes $250,000 a year, more than almost every big-city Mayor in the country. He also kept his taxpayer-funded Mercedes-Benz after slashing $400 million in government jobs and spending."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate but misleading elements with false specifics. Carlos Gimenez did earn roughly $240–$260k as Miami‑Dade County Mayor and faced criticism for budget cuts, but there is no clear evidence he unilaterally approved a 67% pay raise for himself or a self-directed pension hike; reports about a county‑provided Mercedes and budget reductions exist but are taken out of context and conflated with different actions and timeframes. Overall the numeric and causal assertions are not supported as stated.

claim: "Austin is the largest city in the U.S. or Texas with no geographic representation" on its city council.
rationale: Austin has geographically based representation: since 2012 the Austin City Council consists of a mayor elected at-large and ten council members elected from single-member geographic districts. Therefore it is not the largest U.S. or Texas city lacking geographic representation.

claim: A poll conducted in Egypt revealed that 80 percent of Egyptians oppose receiving foreign aid from the United States.
rationale: I could not identify a reputable, specific poll that found exactly 80% of Egyptians oppose receiving U.S. foreign aid. Public-opinion results from Egypt have varied widely by year, pollster, and how the question was phrased, and no widely cited survey reliably supports the precise 80% figure as stated. Without a named poll, date, or methodology, the claim appears to be an unverified or misreported statistic.

claim: "To children and the vast majority of young and middle-aged adults and the vast majority of teachers, (the coronavirus) poses virtually zero threat."
rationale: Risk from SARS-CoV-2 is lower on average for children and younger adults than for older adults, but it is not "virtually zero": children have experienced hospitalizations, deaths, and post-infectious multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS-C); substantial numbers of young and middle-aged adults have been hospitalized or died and can suffer long COVID; teachers have been infected in workplace outbreaks. Population-level surveillance and clinical reports show non-negligible morbidity and mortality across these groups, so the blanket phrase "virtually zero threat" is inaccurate.

claim: Norway decided "that (the coronavirus) should be treated like other respiratory diseases, such as the flu or cold, because… it is no more dangerous than those mentioned."
rationale: Norway did announce moving COVID-19 management into a phase where it is handled like other respiratory illnesses and lifted many restrictions in 2022, but officials justified that shift on high vaccination and population immunity and reduced pressure on health services—not by declaring the virus inherently "no more dangerous" than flu or a cold. Characterizing the decision as based on a conclusion that COVID-19 is as harmless as a cold is a misleading simplification of the government’s cited reasons.

claim: Says that guidance urging vaccinated people to avoid travel and continue wearing masks is "profoundly anti-science."
rationale: Labeling guidance that vaccinated people avoid travel and continue masking as "profoundly anti-science" is inaccurate: such guidance is grounded in scientific evidence about variable vaccine effectiveness against infection and transmission, the existence of breakthrough cases, and evolving variants. Public-health agencies have recommended continued precautions in high-transmission settings as a risk-reduction measure rather than out of anti-scientific motives.

claim: Says Tony Thurmond was "Reprimanded by the Obama Administration for failing to address widespread sexual harassment and assault in district schools."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Obama Administration personally reprimanded Tony Thurmond for failing to address widespread sexual harassment and assault. While federal Office for Civil Rights investigations under the Obama administration sometimes produced findings against school districts, public records and news coverage do not document a federal reprimand directed at Thurmond himself.

claim: Seventy percent of Americans "don't have a college degree."
rationale: U.S. Census Bureau data show roughly 36–40% of adults 25+ hold a bachelor’s degree or higher, so about 60–64% do not — not 70%. The claim overstates the share without a college degree; exact percentages vary by definition and age group but are substantially below 70%.

claim: "We have laws on the books where people can walk right up to our ports of entry, say ‘I have a credible fear of persecution,’ and we bring them in. We don’t send them back."
rationale: Under U.S. immigration law, individuals who present themselves at ports of entry and express a fear of persecution are entitled to a "credible fear" screening; if an asylum officer finds credible fear, the person is referred into full removal proceedings rather than being summarily returned. That statutory and regulatory framework effectively prevents immediate deportation in those cases and allows them to pursue asylum.

claim: Says Bill Gates said, "We need to develop a digital certificate that shows who has received all the vaccinations. Only those with all the required vaccinations may travel, visit churches, participate in sports and music events, get a job, etc."
rationale: No credible record or reliable news source shows Bill Gates uttering that exact statement; fact-checkers have identified the quote as fabricated or misattributed. While Gates has discussed the idea of digital health records or certificates in the context of pandemic response, he did not say this quote advocating blanket exclusion from travel, worship, work, and events.

claim: "Your tellers were paid kickbacks for directing elderly consumers from ... safe deposits to risky ones."
rationale: The claim is a broad, accusatory statement with no named institution, timeframe, evidence, or sources. Allegations that bank tellers were paid kickbacks would typically be documented by regulatory enforcement, lawsuits, or credible reporting; absent such corroboration the statement is unverified and should be treated as false.

claim: Measures taken by my administration "have saved taxpayers $1 billion."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as presented because it lacks any identifying details (which administration, which measures, what timeframe) and no audited or official budget documents are cited to attribute a net $1 billion in taxpayer savings. Fiscal savings claims often rely on projections, accounting choices, or gross rather than net calculations, so without independent verification this specific dollar figure cannot be accepted as fact.

claim: "Black Lives Matter is a terrorist organization."
rationale: The claim is false. Black Lives Matter is a decentralized civil rights movement and affiliated nonprofit organizations; it has not been designated a terrorist organization by the U.S. government, the Department of Justice, the FBI, or major international authorities. While some protests associated with the movement have had instances of violence, isolated incidents do not constitute an official terrorist designation of the movement or its organizations.

claim: "The RI Board of Elections has heard official testimony from Providence residents who claim to have witnessed known illegal aliens voting in local elections."
rationale: There is no public record or credible reporting up to mid-2024 showing the Rhode Island Board of Elections formally received verified testimony from Providence residents that 'known illegal aliens' were observed voting in local elections. While individuals occasionally allege illegal voting at various public meetings, election officials in RI have not substantiated or documented such claims as official findings.

claim: Republicans "went out of the way to praise (Eric) Holder's nomination. ... Not a single Republican senator opposed Eric Holder's nomination."
rationale: This is false. The Senate confirmed Eric Holder as Attorney General in 2009 by a 75–21 roll-call vote, and the votes against his confirmation included multiple Republican senators. Although some Republicans did offer praise for Holder at various points, it is incorrect to say not a single Republican senator opposed his nomination.

claim: 60% of new COVID-19 patients are people who received the vaccine.
rationale: The statement is presented as a universal fact but lacks time, location, variant, and case-definition context; proportions of cases among vaccinated people vary widely by country, vaccine coverage, waning immunity, booster uptake, and circulating variant. Without a specific dataset or timeframe this blanket 60% figure is unsubstantiated and likely misleading even though breakthrough infections do occur and can represent a large share of cases when most people are vaccinated.

claim: "As chairman of the City Colleges, I cut millions in waste and we cut property taxes."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify — it gives no name, dates, or jurisdiction for the claim that as 'chairman of the City Colleges' the speaker cut 'millions in waste' and 'we cut property taxes.' Property tax rates are typically set by city or county authorities (or by a college board's levy subject to broader tax rules), so the claim that a single chairman caused a general property tax cut is not substantiated without documentation of specific board actions, budgets, and tax records.

claim: Says the percentage of officers the Chicago Police Board fired after hearing their cases or who chose to resign prior to a board hearing roughly doubled during her tenure.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it omits who "her" refers to and the exact time period. Without a named official and specific dates, I cannot confirm that the percentage of officers fired or who resigned before hearings "roughly doubled"; such a numeric claim requires checking Chicago Police Board case outcome statistics. Given the missing context I treat the precise assertion as unproven and therefore classify it as false.

claim: "Oregon, once again, remains among the top five hungriest states in the nation."
rationale: State-level food insecurity rankings from USDA and Feeding America typically do not place Oregon in the top five; the highest rates are usually in Southern and Plains states (e.g., Mississippi, Louisiana, New Mexico, Arkansas, Alabama). Oregon's food-insecurity rates in recent years have been lower than those top-five states.

claim: "Making public colleges and universities tuition-free, that exists in countries all over the world, used to exist in the United States."
rationale: Tuition-free public higher education did exist in the United States in various places and periods: many state, municipal and land-grant institutions charged little or no tuition in the 19th and early 20th centuries, and large federal and state programs (for example veterans' GI Bill benefits and state tuition-waiver initiatives) have covered tuition for broad groups. The U.S. did not maintain a single, permanent nationwide free-tuition system for all students, but free or effectively free public colleges have existed historically at the state and local level.

claim: Says Gov. Scott Walker "has caused Wisconsin to lose more jobs than any other state in the country."
rationale: There is no evidence that Wisconsin lost more jobs than any other state as a result of Governor Walker’s policies. State-level employment data (e.g., BLS nonfarm payrolls) do not show Wisconsin experiencing the largest absolute job losses compared with all other states, and job totals are driven by national trends and many local factors, so a singular causal attribution to Walker is unsupported.

claim: Brewpubs can't sell growlers of their beer to customers.
rationale: The statement is too categorical: whether a brewpub can sell growlers depends on local and state alcohol licensing. In many jurisdictions (including numerous U.S. states) brewpubs and breweries are explicitly allowed to sell growlers or other off‑premises containers, while some places restrict growler sales or require additional permits.

claim: The United States has "10,000 IRS agents making sure that you don't take an improper charity deduction," but to fight terrorism, it has "less than two dozen people focusing on countering violent extremism at home."
rationale: The statement bundles two different and misleading claims. While the IRS employs thousands of employees who perform audits and enforcement, there is no clear evidence that 10,000 agents are specifically dedicated to policing charitable deductions; IRS criminal investigators number in the low thousands and audit work is spread across various units. Likewise, responsibility for countering violent extremism is distributed across multiple agencies (FBI, DHS, DOJ and local partners) with far more than “less than two dozen” people working on domestic extremism broadly, so the comparison is inaccurate and misleading.

claim: Says Tony Evers "wants to cut Wisconsin's prison population in half, a dangerous plan that today would mean releasing thousands of violent criminals back into our communities."
rationale: While Governor Tony Evers has supported policies to reduce Wisconsin's prison population, proposals have generally targeted nonviolent offenders, expanded alternatives to incarceration, and reforms to parole and recidivism reduction — not an across‑the‑board half‑prison purge that would release violent criminals. The claim that his plan would "mean releasing thousands of violent criminals" is a misleading extrapolation not supported by his stated policy approaches.

claim: Says Rick Scott "cut $700 million from water management."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable one-time action by Rick Scott that literally cut exactly $700 million from a single "water management" line item. Budget and spending changes during his governorship included vetoes, reassignments, and multi-year adjustments across different water and environmental programs, and independent fact-checkers have characterized blanket $700 million claims as misleading or based on aggregating different funds and years.

claim: In the weekend after the terrorist attacks in Paris, the White House said "this couldn't happen in the United States. ISIS couldn't reach us here."
rationale: There is no record of an official White House statement in the days after the November 2015 Paris attacks saying “this couldn't happen in the United States. ISIS couldn't reach us here.” On the contrary, White House officials publicly acknowledged the threat from ISIS, said there was no specific, credible intelligence of an imminent attack on U.S. soil at that time, and emphasized vigilance and cooperation with French authorities.

claim: "Fox News Sandra Smith: ‘Everybody could see from the United Airlines passenger’s behavior that he was not a genuine American.’ "
rationale: There is no reliable record or transcript showing Fox News anchor Sandra Smith uttering the exact phrase ‘Everybody could see from the United Airlines passenger’s behavior that he was not a genuine American.’ Coverage of United/airline incidents included strong criticism from some Fox personalities, but this specific quote is not documented and appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase. Without a verifiable clip or transcript, the claim that she said those words is unsupported.

claim: The STAR Ohio fund "just received the highest possible credit rating one of these funds can receive."
rationale: The statement claims STAR Ohio "just received" the highest possible credit rating, but there is no verifiable, date-specific evidence provided here. While STAR Ohio has at times held top short-term/money-market designations from agencies, the claim’s timing and which agency’s "highest possible" rating is meant are unclear, so the specific assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: The United States is "the oldest democracy" in the world.
rationale: The claim is false because several political bodies with democratic elements predate the United States. San Marino claims a republican tradition dating to 301 AD and Iceland’s Althing was founded in 930 AD and is often cited as the oldest surviving parliament; the U.S. federal government under the Constitution dates from 1789 (ratified 1788). While the U.S. has one of the world’s oldest written constitutions still in use, it is not the oldest democracy overall.

claim: "(Sen. Robert) Gordon cost us money, exempting the Newark sports arena from paying property taxes and sticking us with the bill."
rationale: The claim misattributes a broad tax exemption decision to a single senator. The Newark arena’s tax treatment was the result of state and local legislative and contractual arrangements (including PILOT/payment-in-lieu deals) reached by multiple officials and entities, not solely enacted by a single Senator Robert Gordon. Additionally, the New Jersey senator named Robert M. Gordon did not represent Newark, making the specific attribution unlikely.

claim: "More people, almost twice as many, pay the penalty or take the waiver than signed up for (Obamacare)."
rationale: This is false. Official CMS enrollment figures (and contemporary fact-checking) show that ACA marketplace enrollment and people covered through the law were larger than the numbers who paid the individual mandate penalty or claimed exemptions; penalty-payers/exemptions were not almost twice as large as enrollees. The claim conflates different measures and time periods to produce a misleading comparison.

claim: In 2010, uninsured voters made up "about 5 percent of the electorate."
rationale: The claim understates the share of uninsured people among voters in 2010. Census and ACS data show roughly mid‑teens uninsured among adults in 2010, and while the uninsured were somewhat less likely to vote than insured adults, that gap would not plausibly shrink their share of the electorate to as low as 5 percent. Contemporary post‑election surveys and fact‑checks found the uninsured made up a noticeably larger portion of the voting population than 5 percent.

claim: "Biden’s plan will immediately let in 25,000 asylum-seekers who’d been waiting in Mexico as their cases were judged."
rationale: The administration’s announced asylum/processing proposals did not result in an immediate admission of 25,000 people who had been waiting in Mexico. Statements and plans discussed setting processing capacity or creating enrollment slots (or monthly limits) and restarting complex court or parole procedures, but they did not equate to an immediate, one-time release of 25,000 MPP asylum-seekers into the U.S.

claim: Since being elected in 2002, Scott Walker has "given back over $370,000 of his salary to the county."
rationale: Contemporary news reports and county payroll records from his time as Milwaukee County Executive indicate Scott Walker voluntarily returned portions of his salary, with totals reported at about $370,000 over his tenure beginning in 2002. Multiple fact-checks and local outlets corroborated a figure in that range.

claim: "States with the most gun laws tend to have the fewest gun deaths."
rationale: Multiple state-level analyses and reviews find that states with more comprehensive gun-safety laws generally have lower firearm death rates than states with fewer laws. These findings are based on observational comparisons and meta-analyses, though the strength of the association varies by type of firearm death (homicide vs. suicide) and study design.

claim: Planned Parenthood clinics are "closing down all over the country" because Roe v. Wade was overturned.
rationale: While some Planned Parenthood health centers stopped providing abortions or temporarily paused services in states with post-Dobbs bans, there is no evidence that clinics are "closing down all over the country." Closures and service changes have been localized to states that enacted near-total abortion bans, and many Planned Parenthood clinics remain open and continue offering non-abortion reproductive health services nationwide.

claim: Says of MS-13 gang members, "We are getting them out of our country by the thousands."
rationale: The quoted line matches public statements made by former President Donald Trump and other officials who repeatedly said they were removing MS-13 members "by the thousands." Multiple speeches and tweets from 2017–2019 include near-identical wording asserting thousands of removals. Exact counts and who qualifies as MS-13 can vary, but the statement accurately reflects what was said.

claim: "Greg Abbott said it would be a ‘waste’ to expand pre-k to all Texas children."
rationale: Governor Greg Abbott publicly opposed expanding pre-K to all Texas children and characterized universal expansion as a waste or a wasteful use of taxpayer dollars, arguing funds would go to families who do not need them. That characterization appeared in his statements during legislative debate and media remarks criticizing universal pre-K proposals.

claim: Says the late Lady Bird Johnson sicced the CIA on actress and singer Eartha Kitt after Kitt spoke out against the Vietnam War during a White House luncheon in January 1968.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Lady Bird Johnson formally 'sicced the CIA' on Eartha Kitt after Kitt's January 1968 White House remarks. Contemporary reporting and later histories document that Kitt was publicly denounced, lost work, and faced government scrutiny, but domestic investigations of dissidents at the time were usually handled by the FBI (COINTELPRO), and CIA involvement in domestic targeting would have been highly irregular and is not substantiated by records.

claim: In the case of a catastrophic event, the Atlanta-area offices of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention will self-destruct.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official policy indicating that the CDC's Atlanta-area offices contain self-destruct mechanisms. The agency's publicly known emergency planning emphasizes continuity of operations, evacuation, and security — not deliberate destruction of its facilities, which would pose obvious safety and legal issues.

claim: "We have developed a wind industry (in Washington state) from zero to $6 billion in 12 years."
rationale: The claim is unsupported and likely false because Washington state had commercial wind development well before the last 12 years (for example, the Stateline Wind project began operations around 1999), so the industry did not grow "from zero." In addition, the statement provides no clear metric (annual revenue, cumulative investment, or economic output) and I am not aware of authoritative state or federal data confirming a $6 billion increase attributed exactly to Washington's wind industry over a 12‑year span.

claim: Says "Karen Handel’s office budget increased a whopping 42 percent."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which office and which years are meant, and I find no clear, publicly recorded evidence that any office Karen Handel held experienced a 42% budget increase attributable to her. Public office budgets (e.g., state secretary of state or congressional office budgets) are set by legislatures and appropriations and are a matter of public record; without a specific timeframe or source, the statement is unsupported and misleading. If a particular year or office is specified, records could confirm or refute a precise percentage change.

claim: Says a pandemic occurs exactly every 100 years.
rationale: There is no evidence that pandemics follow a strict 100-year cycle. Historical pandemics (e.g., Black Death in the 1300s, 1918 influenza, 1957 and 1968 influenzas, 2009 H1N1, and COVID-19 in 2019) occur irregularly, driven by pathogen evolution and social factors, not a fixed periodicity.

claim: Unvaccinated people "are making the vaccinated people sick and die, but the unvaccinated people are not dead or sick."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate: unvaccinated people have higher rates of infection, hospitalization, and death for vaccine-preventable diseases (e.g., COVID-19) while vaccinated people have substantially lower risks. Although unvaccinated individuals can increase community transmission and contribute to breakthrough infections among the vaccinated, many unvaccinated people also become seriously ill or die; vaccinated breakthrough cases are generally much less severe.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to kick thousands of kids off of BadgerCare."
rationale: There is no record of Donald Trump explicitly saying he 'wants to kick thousands of kids off of BadgerCare.' Trump has supported Medicaid changes (waivers, work requirements, block grants/per‑capita caps) that critics say could reduce enrollment in programs like Wisconsin's BadgerCare, but that is a policy consequence rather than a documented stated intent to remove children from the program.

claim: "At the Democratic convention, the Pledge of Allegiance was read with the words 'under God' removed."
rationale: Fact-checking found this claim to be misleading. At the 2020 Democratic National Convention a filmed pledge segment circulated that in some edited clips lacked the words 'under God,' but the omission was due to editing choices and how individual children recited the lines rather than an official decision by the convention to remove the phrase. There is no evidence the DNC formally excised 'under God' from the Pledge.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "put Planned Parenthood on a state medical board but failed to put a pro-life group on the same board."
rationale: There is no clear, documented evidence that Governor Mitt Romney explicitly 'put Planned Parenthood on a state medical board' as an organizational appointment while denying a slot to a pro‑life group. State medical boards typically appoint individual licensed professionals or public members, and contemporary reporting and appointment records do not corroborate this specific claim. Without named board, dates, or appointees the statement reads like a misleading or unverified allegation.

claim: "Corona is so bad, this guy died twice!"
rationale: The statement asserts a person 'died twice' from coronavirus, which is not supported by verifiable evidence. Medical death is ordinarily irreversible; reports sometimes describe mistaken death declarations or successful resuscitations after clinical arrest, but those are not instances of someone biologically dying twice. Without a specific, credible case, the claim is misleading or false.

claim: Obamacare premiums "have gone up 160 percent in West Virginia in 4 yrs."
rationale: The claim is misleading or false as stated because premium changes under the ACA vary greatly by year, plan metal level, insurer and county; a 160% increase is a cherry-picked figure that likely refers to a specific plan or short interval rather than the statewide benchmark or average. Independent fact-checkers have found similar broad statements about 'Obamacare premiums' often omit that many consumers receive tax credits that offset increases and that statewide average benchmark premiums did not uniformly rise by 160% over a four-year span.

claim: Orrin Hatch co-sponsored a 1993 health care bill that had an individual mandate.
rationale: There is no reliable record that Senator Orrin Hatch co-sponsored any 1993 federal health-care bill that included an individual mandate. Hatch was not a sponsor of the Clinton-era Health Security Act and his Senate record does not show him backing a federal individual mandate in 1993; claims to the contrary appear to conflate different proposals or years.

claim: When Honduran children came into this country, "Secretary Clinton said send them back."
rationale: There is no credible record of Secretary Hillary Clinton saying the quoted phrase "send them back" about Honduran children entering the U.S. Public statements and reporting from the period emphasize humane treatment, regional cooperation, and calls for immigration reform rather than an explicit order to "send them back." The claim appears to be a misattribution or a misleading paraphrase.

claim: "We don't need a separate (prescription drug) database ... Pharmacies already have a database in place."
rationale: Pharmacies do maintain internal dispensing records and many chains run their own databases, but those systems are private, fragmented across vendors and companies, and are not a single, standardized, universally accessible prescription database. For purposes like centralized monitoring, public reporting, price transparency, or cross-state tracking, pharmacy systems are not an adequate substitute for a separate, centralized or regulatory database.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Paul Ryan promised to "end health care for our seniors."
rationale: Paul Ryan did not promise to “end health care for our seniors.” His public budget proposals advocated restructuring Medicare (e.g., premium-support/voucher-style changes and spending caps) and reducing the federal guarantee, but he framed these as reforms rather than an explicit pledge to end senior health care. Critics characterized those reforms as effectively ending guaranteed benefits, but that is an interpretation rather than a direct promise.

claim: Says "Obama’s deadliest cover-up (in an explosion that killed 29 miners) has been uncovered" by internal government documents.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Obama or his administration orchestrated a deliberate cover-up of an explosion that killed 29 miners. The April 2010 Upper Big Branch mine disaster in West Virginia was extensively investigated by MSHA and the Department of Justice, and led to regulatory findings and criminal charges against company officials rather than evidence of an Obama-led concealment. Media reporting about internal documents highlighted enforcement failures and agency lapses, not a presidential cover-up.

claim: "The federal government is now on track" for the second-largest budget deficit "in 65 years."
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or source and is not supported by publicly available Treasury and CBO data: the largest recent U.S. deficits were in 2020 and 2021 (COVID-era), and more recent deficits, while large, do not clearly rank as the "second-largest in 65 years" without additional context or a specific fiscal-year projection. Because the statement is ambiguous about which year or measure (nominal dollars vs. percent of GDP) it is misleading and likely incorrect as stated.

claim: Says Thom Tillis "refuses to say what we should do to combat ISIS."
rationale: The claim asserts that Thom Tillis "refuses to say what we should do to combat ISIS," but public record shows Tillis has repeatedly articulated positions on confronting ISIS (supporting military action, aid to allies, and increased counterterrorism funding) rather than categorically refusing to state a course of action. Without a specific time, question, or quotation showing a refusal, the blanket statement is unsupported. It appears to conflate political criticism with an absolute refusal to state policy.

claim: Under Hillary Clinton’s plan "illegal immigrants convicted of committing crimes get to stay."
rationale: Hillary Clinton’s immigration proposals did not say that undocumented immigrants convicted of crimes could remain without consequence. Her campaign emphasized prioritizing removal of those convicted of serious or violent crimes and proposed that legalization pathways exclude people with serious criminal records, while offering relief and a path to citizenship for certain groups (e.g., DACA recipients) who generally lack serious convictions. The claim mischaracterizes those distinctions and implies a blanket protection for criminal offenders that her plan did not provide.

claim: It is a "myth" that "per-student funding only rose by 47 cents this year."
rationale: The statement labels as a 'myth' that per-student funding only rose by 47 cents, but it gives no jurisdiction, year, or whether figures are nominal or inflation-adjusted, so the blanket claim cannot be verified. Per-pupil funding changes vary widely by state and district and depend on whether one counts only state funds, total funds, or one-time federal allocations; some places saw larger nominal or real increases and others saw declines. Without specific data, calling the 47-cent figure a myth is not supportable.

claim: "U.S. Department of Homeland Security has told banks -- in writing -- it may inspect safe deposit boxes without warrant and seize any gold, silver, guns or other valuables it finds inside those boxes!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Department of Homeland Security issued a written order telling banks they may inspect safe-deposit boxes without a warrant and seize valuables. U.S. legal practice and the Fourth Amendment generally require a warrant or clear exigent circumstances for searches and seizures, and reputable checks of the claim have found no DHS policy authorizing blanket warrantless inspections of private safe-deposit boxes.

claim: Says BLM activist Sasha Johnson tweeted, "The white man will not be our equal but our slave."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Sasha Johnson posted that tweet. After the claim circulated, journalists and fact‑checking organizations found the hostile tweet circulated in screenshots was either from a different or unauthenticated account and Johnson and her supporters denied she authored it.

claim: Says that under the law, New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio "can’t open" the city’s schools.
rationale: This is misleading. The New York City mayor directs the NYC Department of Education and has substantial authority over operating city schools, but those actions are constrained by state education law, state or city public-health orders, court rulings, and collective bargaining agreements. Saying he "can't open" the schools as an absolute legal rule is incorrect without specifying a particular court order or emergency directive.

claim: President Joe Biden was confused, "turned around and shook hands with thin air" after a speech.
rationale: Short video clips circulated showing President Biden reaching out after a speech and appearing to shake no one, but context and fuller footage indicate he was reaching toward a person or staff member who had already moved or been obscured, not demonstrably confused. Calling the moment proof that he was 'confused' is speculative and not supported by reliable, full-context reporting.

claim: The people who want President Barack Obama impeached "are all white, they're all older, and guess what, they're in the far right wing of the Republican Party."
rationale: The claim asserts a universal characterization ("all white, all older, ... in the far right") which is false. Polling and public records from the Obama years show that support for impeachment was concentrated among Republicans and skewed older, but it was not exclusively white or exclusively older, nor limited solely to the political far right — there were supporters across age ranges and some nonwhite supporters, and calls for impeachment came from both hard-right activists and some mainstream Republican figures.

claim: "(Texas Republicans) believe in abolishing Social Security, abolishing V.A. health care."
rationale: The statement overgeneralizes: while some individual Texas Republicans and conservative activists have called for privatizing or reforming Social Security or reducing veterans programs, there is no consistent, statewide Republican position that calls for outright abolition of Social Security and VA health care. Many Texas Republican officials defend or seek to reform rather than abolish these programs.

claim: Countries with a higher minimum wage than the United States’ $7.25 an hour include Denmark at $21, Australia at $15.81, Germany at $11 and France at $12.35.
rationale: The US federal minimum is $7.25/hr, but the claim is inaccurate because Denmark does not have a statutory national minimum wage (wages are set by collective bargaining), so listing it as $21 is misleading. The numeric figures for Germany and France also do not match current statutory rates (Germany has a statutory €12/hr minimum and France’s SMIC is set in euros and its USD equivalent varies), though Australia does have a national minimum wage roughly in the stated USD range depending on exchange rates.

claim: Says Tammy Baldwin's record includes "opposing harsher punishments for criminals who commit violent crimes near schools."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Tammy Baldwin has a record of specifically opposing laws that impose harsher punishments for violent crimes committed near schools. While Baldwin has supported criminal-justice reform and opposed broad mandatory minimums and some sentencing enhancements, that general stance is not the same as a documented vote or public position against school-proximity penalty enhancements. Without a specific bill or vote cited, the claim overstates available evidence.

claim: The "48, 49 percent" that supports President Barack Obama are "people who pay no income tax."
rationale: This claim conflates two different statistics. The roughly 47–49% figure has been used to describe the share of households in a given year that owed no federal income tax, but Obama supporters were a broad coalition that included many people who do pay federal income tax; exit polls and tax-data comparisons show his voters spanned income and tax-paying status. It is therefore incorrect to say that the 48–49% who support Obama are people who pay no income tax.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton called the Trans-Pacific Partnership "the gold standard. You called it the gold standard of trade deals. You said it’s the finest deal you’ve ever seen."
rationale: Hillary Clinton publicly praised the Trans-Pacific Partnership during 2015, characterizing it as the “gold standard” for trade agreements and speaking positively about its provisions. Multiple speeches and news reports from her 2015-2016 campaign quote her using that phrasing or very similar language to describe the TPP.

claim: "One of the reasons that Social Security is in so much trouble is that the only funding stream comes from people who get a wage. The people who get wages is declining dramatically."
rationale: It is true that Social Security’s primary ongoing revenue comes from payroll taxes on wages, but the claim that the number of people receiving wages is "declining dramatically" is incorrect. Total employment and numbers of wage earners in the U.S. have generally grown with population, though the worker-to-beneficiary ratio has fallen over decades because of aging (more retirees per worker). The statement conflates a slower-growing worker base and demographic pressure with a dramatic decline in wage earners.

claim: "Donald Trump is appealing as much to Democrats as he is to Republicans."
rationale: National polls, party identification, and election results consistently show much higher favorability and vote intention for Donald Trump among Republicans than among Democrats. While a small minority of Democrats may express support for or sympathy with him on particular issues, overall he does not attract equal appeal across the two parties.

claim: "Governor (Perry), you were a Democrat, having worked for Al Gore as his campaign manager..."
rationale: The claim bundles two assertions: Rick Perry was once a Democrat early in his career but long ago switched to the Republican Party, and that he worked as Al Gore's campaign manager. While Perry did have Democratic affiliation early on, there is no evidence he ever served as Al Gore's campaign manager or worked for Gore’s presidential campaigns. The specific assertion that he was Gore’s campaign manager is false.

claim: "We're spending millions for each individual" held at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.
rationale: The claim is too broad and omits timeframe and basis for ‘millions.’ Public Department of Defense and Congressional Research Service figures show Guantánamo’s annual operating costs divided by the detainee population have in some years amounted to roughly about $1 million per detainee per year, but not typically multiple millions per individual without additional context (e.g., long‑term lifecycle or transfer costs). Saying categorically “we're spending millions for each individual” is misleading without specifying the period, cost categories, and whether it is per year or cumulative.

claim: Says Sen. Tim Kaine "approves of and even applauds his son's participation in a known terrorist organization, #Antifa."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Sen. Tim Kaine publicly 'approves of and even applauds' his son's participation in Antifa. Public reporting and Kaine's statements have emphasized respecting his adult son's right to protest and have not framed his son as a member of a formal terrorist organization. Additionally, 'Antifa' is a decentralized movement rather than a designated terrorist organization.

claim: "Republicans want to restore #gunrights to felons"
rationale: The claim presents a universal GOP position, but Republicans are not uniformly advocating restoration of gun rights to all felons. While many Republican lawmakers and Republican-led states have backed measures to restore firearm rights in specific cases (for example after sentence completion, for non-violent offenders, or via pardons/expungements), others oppose restoring rights to violent or certain felons; there is no single party-wide mandate to restore gun rights to felons generally.

claim: U.S. Rep. Scott Rigell "wants gun owners in a federal registration system."
rationale: There is no credible record of Rep. Scott Rigell advocating for a federal gun-owner registration system. His public record and statements while in Congress aligned with pro-Second Amendment positions and opposition to federal gun registries, and he did not sponsor or endorse legislation creating a national registry of gun owners. The claim appears to mischaracterize his stance or conflate other proposals (like background checks) with a universal registration mandate.

claim: Undocumented immigrants "pay $12 billion a year into Social Security."
rationale: Multiple government and research estimates (notably a Social Security Administration analysis of 2010 data) found that unauthorized/undocumented workers paid roughly $12–13 billion in payroll taxes into Social Security in that year. The exact annual figure varies by year and methodology, but saying they pay about $12 billion a year is consistent with published estimates for at least recent past years.

claim: "The Green New Deal would require that 99% of homes in the country be torn down and rebuilt more ‘energy efficient’ over a ten year period."
rationale: The Green New Deal resolution does not require tearing down 99% of homes over ten years. Its text calls for upgrading or retrofitting existing buildings and sets broad climate and infrastructure goals; it is a non-binding framework rather than a specific law mandating mass demolition. Multiple fact-checks have debunked the 99% teardown claim as a mischaracterization.

claim: "Drone technology now allows an individual to be recorded in their homes by drones as small as birds and immediately uploaded to the internet."
rationale: Small consumer and specialized micro‑UAVs exist that are comparable in size to birds and commonly carry small cameras. Many such drones can fly indoors if they gain access and support live wireless or cellular video links, enabling recorded footage to be uploaded or streamed to the internet in real time, though practical limits (battery, obstructions) apply.

claim: Dollar General "added 2,500 stores and 20,000 jobs" during his four-year tenure as CEO.
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported as stated: it fails to identify which CEO or the exact four-year period, and public company reports and press coverage show varying store- and employment-growth figures that do not clearly match '2,500 stores and 20,000 jobs' for a single four-year CEO term. Without a specified timeframe the numbers are misleading and cannot be verified as accurate for a particular four-year tenure.

claim: "The vaccination campaign" increased COVID-19 deaths by 175% in one year.
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and implausible as stated: large bodies of evidence from clinical trials and real-world surveillance show COVID-19 vaccines reduce risk of severe illness and death, and there is no credible evidence that vaccination campaigns caused a 175% increase in COVID-19 deaths in any defined population. Reported rises in deaths in some places and times were attributable to factors such as new variants, waning immunity, changes in testing/reporting, or low vaccine uptake, not causal effects of vaccination itself.

claim: Says when he was governor, "most of the Democrats" voted for his billion-dollar property-tax cuts, but U.S. Senate rival Tammy Baldwin "voted against it."
rationale: The claim is misleading on two counts: federal officials like Tammy Baldwin do not vote on state budget or property-tax bills, so she could not have cast a direct vote for or against a Wisconsin governor's state tax measure. In Wisconsin, major bipartisan support by "most Democrats" for the governor's large, multi‑billion‑dollar property‑tax cuts is not supported by legislative voting patterns—Republican majorities carried Walker's major tax measures while many Democrats opposed them (though some Democrats supported smaller, targeted relief measures).

claim: "Over 73% of all donations raised (from the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge) are going to fundraising, overhead, executive salaries, and external donations."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that more than 73% of Ice Bucket Challenge donations were consumed by fundraising, overhead, executive pay, and external donations. Public reporting on the 2014 campaign (which raised roughly $100–115M) and the ALS Association’s audited statements and charity evaluators show substantial shares were directed to research grants, patient services, and program work; while administrative and fundraising costs existed and some grants went to other organizations, the claim’s specific >73% figure is unsupported and implausible.

claim: Gov. Lincoln Chafee has imposed "a mandatory abortion fee" on all Rhode Islanders who buy health insurance through the state’s Obamacare exchange.
rationale: There is no evidence that Gov. Lincoln Chafee imposed a universal “mandatory abortion fee” on all purchasers through Rhode Island’s ACA exchange. Under federal and state rules, abortion coverage (when offered) must be funded via separately charged premiums or segregated accounts; only people who elect plans or riders that include abortion would pay for that coverage.
